When projecting your portfolio growth for retirement planning, use real (inflation-adjusted) returns of 6-7% rather than nominal returns of 9-10%. A $1 million nominal balance in 30 years has the purchasing power of roughly $550,000 in today's dollars at 2% average inflation. Planning with real returns ensures you are targeting a portfolio that can actually support your desired spending level.

Track your actual spending for 3 months and annualize it. Multiply by 25 to get your FI number using the 4% safe withdrawal rate. If you spend $60,000 per year, your FI number is $1,500,000.

Add up all retirement accounts (401k, IRA, Roth IRA, HSA), taxable brokerage accounts, and savings. Exclude home equity and non-liquid assets. This is your starting balance for the future value calculation.

Subtract your monthly spending from your monthly after-tax income. Include employer 401(k) match and any other automatic savings. This is your periodic contribution amount for the future value formula.

Use the future value of a lump sum plus annuity formula, or a simple online calculator, to project when your current balance plus monthly contributions will reach your FI number. Use 7% real return (after inflation) for conservative planning.

Test what happens if you increase contributions by $200/month, $500/month, or $1,000/month. Seeing the concrete impact of a savings rate increase — often shaving 2-5 years off your FI timeline — makes the trade-offs tangible and motivating.

For long-term stock market projections, use 7% for inflation-adjusted (real) returns or 10% for nominal returns based on the S&P 500 historical average. For a more conservative estimate, use 6% real. For bond-heavy portfolios, use 3-4% real. Always specify whether you are using nominal or real returns — mixing them up is one of the most common planning mistakes.

Future value calculations show what WOULD happen if returns were constant every year. In reality, markets fluctuate — you might earn 25% one year and lose 15% the next. Over 20-30 year periods, average returns tend to converge toward historical norms, making future value projections reasonably useful for planning. Treat them as directional estimates, not guarantees.

Future value asks: "What will $10,000 today be worth in 20 years?" Present value asks the reverse: "What is $50,000 in 20 years worth in today's dollars?" They use the same variables but in opposite directions. Present value is useful for evaluating whether a future payout (like a pension or annuity) is worth the cost today.

The Rule of 72 works for any compounding rate, including inflation. At 3% inflation, prices double every 24 years (72 / 3 = 24). This means $50,000 in annual spending today becomes $100,000 in 24 years in nominal terms — your purchasing power is halved if your income stays flat. This is why investing in assets that outpace inflation is essential.

For FI planning, future value is more intuitive — it tells you what your portfolio will grow to. However, the most practical approach is to calculate future value using real (after-inflation) returns. This effectively gives you a future value stated in today's purchasing power, which is what you actually need to know for spending planning.

In tax-advantaged accounts (401k, IRA, Roth IRA, HSA), your investments compound without tax drag, so the standard future value formula works directly. In taxable accounts, capital gains taxes, dividend taxes, and tax-loss harvesting all affect your real return. A rough adjustment is to reduce your assumed return by 0.5-1.0% for taxable accounts to account for ongoing tax drag.

Future value calculations are the most practical tool in the FI planner's toolkit. They turn abstract concepts like compound growth and savings rate into concrete dollar amounts and specific timelines. The key takeaways are straightforward: use 7% real returns for conservative planning, always account for inflation by using real rather than nominal returns, and remember that your monthly contribution rate has a far larger impact on the outcome than chasing an extra point or two of return. The Rule of 72 gives you instant mental math for any investment decision — how long to double, what rate you need, and how inflation erodes purchasing power. Combined with a clear FI number and a disciplined savings rate, future value projections show you exactly when financial independence becomes reality. Run the numbers, test different scenarios, and let the math motivate you to increase that monthly contribution whenever you can.

#9041. Pair accused of murdering South African artist and curator Tamlin Blake appear in court as art scene mourns

As well as her work as an artist, Tamlin Blake was the chief curator for the Spier Arts Trust, a Cape Town-based organisation dedicated to building sustainable careers for professional artists

Two men accused of the murder of the South African mixed-media artist and curator Tamlin Blake appeared in the Riebeek West magistrate’s court on Wednesday (25 November). Blake was found killed on Sunday at her home in Riebeek-West, a small town 80km northwest of Cape Town. The 51-year-old artist was a well-loved member of the town’s prominent community of artists, among whom she lived for the past 20 years.

The two suspects, Pedro Fraser and Ronnie Von Wielligh, both aged 32, have been charged with murder and possession of stolen goods and will appear in court again on 1 December where they are expected to respond to the charges.

Angry protestors gathered outside the court, demanding justice with some chanting “no bail!”, reported the South African digital news platform, News24.

A representative for the state told the court that the murder was a Schedule 6 offence, which is one of the most serious categories of crime, according to News24. Prosecutors reportedly said she was attacked with a sharp object. Fraser and Von Wielligh will remain in prison until their appearance next Tuesday.

The police tracked down the suspects after tracing Blake’s cellphone, which was allegedly stolen during the attack, a source told another news platform, IOL Media.

“One suspect was arrested in possession of the cellphone. During police questioning, he admitted that he did not commit the offence alone. He then took police to his co-accused,” IOL Media’s source said.

The residents of Riebeek West and neighbouring Riebeek Kasteel are “completely shell shocked” by the news of Blake’s death, a fellow local artist and close friend of Blake’s, Kevan Moses, tells The Art Newspaper. He describes the area as home to many artists, “international, established as well as new” and that it is a “very nurturing creative environment”.

Blake, who was born in Johannesburg, obtained a master’s in fine arts at the University of Stellenbosch in 2001. She has exhibited extensively at home and abroad and is represented by Everard Read Gallery, which has locations in South Africa and London.

Blake was, according to her website, instrumental in developing beading techniques which are now used by various South African artists. Her recent works include tapestries woven from recycled hand-spun newspaper. She was also the chief curator for the Spier Arts Trust, a Cape Town-based organisation dedicated to building sustainable careers for professional artists. There Blake oversaw the acquisition of works of art for diverse collections and lead initiatives that supported artists at pivotal stages of their careers.

“Tamlin was a remarkable artist whose work reflected a deep sensitivity to the natural world and an unwavering commitment to her creative practice,” Everard Read Gallery said in a statement. “Through her distinctive voice and vision, she built a respected career and touched the lives of collectors, colleagues, and fellow artists in South Africa and abroad.

“We are grateful to have worked with Tamlin over many years, and to have shared her work with our audiences. Her contribution to contemporary South African art will be remembered with admiration, gratitude and affection.”

Spier Arts Trust described Blake in a statement as a “visionary artist” who “possessed the rarest gift: a boundless, ego-free generosity that put other people’s growth and dignity at the centre of her life’s work”.

“Those of us fortunate enough to have worked alongside her will forever remember her sharp eye, her quiet grace, her advocacy for authentic, exceptional expression, and the warmth she brought into every studio conversation,” the trust said.

Her friend Moses said: “Tamlin was a great artist, the gentlest person and a quiet thought leader. She was a mentor for many artists. She will be truly missed.”

Blake leaves behind her husband and two daughters, aged 18 and 20.

#9040. Domes depict constellations of missiles in the night sky at Sharjah Architecture Triennial

Architect Mohamad Nahleh and architecture professor Ozayr Saloojee have created three domed structures that reimagine constellations by mapping military objects in the night sky, which were displayed at this year’s Sharjah Architecture Triennial.

Titled After Night There is Nothing, the trio of installations aim to bring attention to how communities are responding to drones, satellites, rockets and missiles changing the sky above them.

Covered in thatch, the three curved wood-and-steel structures are segments of a giant globe.

Vinyl lines the inner curves, where Nahleh and Saloojee designed creature-like constellations based on man-made military objects in the sky.

The trio of installations were displayed at three venues at the Sharjah Architecture Triennial – the Al Qasimiyah School, a former slaughterhouse, and in the sandy Al Madam town.

“This is ‘night sky optimism’ – optimism through catastrophe,” Nahleh told Dezeen. “The night sky we are talking about in this project is not the sky of beautiful stars and constellations, but the contemporary sky filled with drones, satellites, rockets and missiles that are changing the way we understand the sky above us.”

“The drones, missiles, rockets and satellites eclipse some of the constellations, and sometimes fuse with them,” he continued.

“That fusion is at the heart of this project – how do these technologies, through cultural practices on the ground, begin to morph into new creatures and new constellations that people try to make sense of to interpret the violence of this military technology that is taking place.”

Nahleh and Saloojee aimed to combine the reality of modern war with mythical storytelling, drawing upon their research into communities exposed to military attacks.

“We have noticed in our research that, especially in geographies witnessing prolonged violence, these objects are producing new mythical creatures – creatures that fuse together technological advancement with epistemic practices and myth-making practices that happen from the ground,” said Nahleh.

“Most of these creatures, these modern constellations as we’re calling them, are populating the night sky in our drawing alongside pathways of flights of drones, satellites and other things that manifest across the night sky we’ve inherited, rather than the one we lost,” he continued.

“We think of these creatures as ones that attempt to tame the military brightness that is populating the sky around us, be it in the shape of missiles, phosphorus, or flares.”

As well as depicting creature-like constellations in their inner curves, the structures themselves were designed as creatures – the nocturnal Solifugi spider known to run out the sun and into shade.

“The project is dedicated to the Solifugi, which is a spider that by nature runs away from the sun, the sun of imperial savagery,” said Nahleh. “It has a very thick skin to protect it from this brightness, and in its belly is a map of the contemporary sky.”

Three openings puncture the shell in each of the installations. In the desert site at Al Madam, a vertical cut-out frames a view of the minaret of a distant mosque, and at the slaughterhouse site, a long opening was set at the height of a cow.

Traditional Hakawati storytellers will narrate stories at the installations as part of the triennial, which runs until April.

“The story is difficult, but it’s about finding optimism,” said Nahleh. “People are carving their own histories on the weapons that are here to annihilate them.”

“There’s a paradox here that we have to confront,” he continued. “When libraries are being erased, and people have no more books to publish or things to write on, they’re writing on the weapons that are sent to devour them.”

“Kids now are finding ways again to dream by placing their wishes upon the shooting stars, which are usually missiles and rockets. It’s a sad and complicated story, but we can no longer escape it by wishing for a sky we no longer have.”

We rounded up eight highlights from this year’s Sharjah Architecture Triennial, which includes a draping shelter that pays homage to the improvised learning spaces created by Virginia’s Black community, and a circular canopy with cut-outs that plot 41 medieval Arabic poetic names for the sun.

Sharjah Architecture Triennial 2026 takes place from 14 November 2026 to 14 April 2027 at various locations across Sharjah, UAE. See Dezeen Events Guide for an up-to-date list of architecture and design events taking place around the world.

#9039. Alien Breed 35th Anniversary Collection review: A brilliant slice of gaming history

Alien Breed 35th Anniversary Collection is a fascinating archive of Team17's early years, filled with art and developer insights, even if not all the games deserve a return visit.

Six Amiga-era Alien Breed games in one package

Virtual Museum is packed with art, interviews and unreleased projects

Twin-stick controls, CRT filters and save states

Local co-op, online Rush Mode and solo Horde Mode

The 3D games feel like historical curiosities

Early top-down games can be punishingly difficult

Why you can trust Creative Bloq Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.

Format: PS5 (reviewed), Xbox Series X/S, PC

How to buy: Digitally on the PS Store, Xbox Store, Steam

Some games you remember as brilliant, and others you remember as brilliant because you were 12, sitting in front of an Amiga with a joystick in one hand and a pile of floppy disks beside you. Alien Breed is probably a bit of both.

Team17's sci-fi shooter celebrates its 35th anniversary with this new collection, bringing together six games from the series' original Amiga era (read my Apidya review for more Amiga gaming). That's quite a lot of history in one package, taking in the original top-down shooters and the later, more ambitious attempts to bring the series into the 3D era.

And there's a lot to like about the way this collection has been assembled. Alongside the games is an interactive archive filled with original artwork, developer interviews, soundtracks, design documents and even material from Alien Breed projects that never made it to release. It's a proper look back at a British studio finding its feet during one of gaming's most interesting periods.

But one question hangs over it all: are these games still fun to play?

The collection includes Alien Breed (1991), Alien Breed: Special Edition '92, Alien Breed II: The Horror Continues, Alien Breed: Tower Assault, Alien Breed 3D and Alien Breed 3D II: The Killing Grounds.

The first four are the games most people will remember, and I played more of the classic top-down 2D shooters, with their overhead perspective, maze-like levels, and hordes of aliens waiting around every corner. There's a little Gauntlet in the DNA, a bit of Smash TV, and more than a hint of James Cameron's Aliens. You explore abandoned space stations, collect ammunition, hunt for keys, and try not to get overwhelmed by the growing number of creatures closing in, often because of a brutal respawn system.

It's a simple formula, but Team17 – now a publisher of some of the best indie games – knew how to make it entertaining. There's a nice rhythm to working through a level, finding supplies and opening up new areas, although the difficulty can be pretty unforgiving.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

Playing those early games now in the 35th Anniversary Collection showcases both the strengths and weaknesses of the series. These games are brutally fun when you take time to learn the maps, play and replay, remember where keys are located, and manage the alien 'breed' and its AI by keeping it locked behind corridor walls.

But it can also become overburdened by the horde; without the right weapons, life is short-lived, and it can be frustrating to waste keys and then not be able to unlock the doors you need, and restart beckons. The original is worse for this; the Special Edition improved, and by Alien Breed II the team had ironed out the kinks, and the game plays with a perfect rhythm. Back in the 90s, we had to play two games and three years to get perfection; on this collection, it's right there.

Some may disagree; I think Alien Breed II, with its visual detail and balanced map design and item placement, is the best of the series, but Tower Assault comes close. The environments offer more variety and a stronger sense of progression, but the second game is the real gem.

Then there's the move into 3D, something I envied back in the day because you needed an Amiga 1200 or Amiga CD32 to run it. Alien Breed 3D arrived in 1995, when everyone wanted to make a Doom-like shooter, and Team17 was keen to prove the Amiga could compete with the growing PC gaming setups and new consoles like PlayStation. It was an ambitious move, especially given the hardware limitations, and the sequel, The Killing Grounds, pushed that idea further but, interestingly, dropped much of the Alien Breed branding and imagery for a more Doom-like aesthetic.

Playing them now is a different experience because a) I can play them and b) they're important games in the story of the Amiga. But being historically interesting and being enjoyable shooters are two very different things.

Alien Breed 3D now feels like a tech demo, and it drops much of the series' identity: the 3D experience. I remember the impact this game had back in '95, especially for Amiga owners used to pushing the computer's graphics to the limit. But is it a good game? Not really. It's a decent Doom clone, but even in '95 it couldn't compete with games like Dark Forces.

Alien Breed 3D II is slightly different, though: it plays better today and has a cleaner, more focused Doom-like appeal, but much of Alien Breed's visual hooks and identity have been ironed out in favour of what feels like a solid, standalone Doom clone.

But playing all the games back to back in the 35th Anniversary Collection is more interesting than just replaying games I loved on my Amiga, because it shows how a series develops, how improvements are inched forward, how trends and pressures pull on a brand and force new directions. This is where the collection excels.

If you're buying this collection purely for the games, you might be missing its biggest selling point.

The Virtual Museum is an interactive archive that lets you explore the history of Alien Breed through original box art, advertising, concept work, soundtracks and interviews with the people who made the games. It also includes a timeline and material from projects that never saw the light of day, which I've spent far more time exploring than I imagined. It includes a cancelled PSP game that looks like it could have struck the right balance between 'modern' 3D and classic Alien Breed corridor shootouts, and an Alien Breed RTS that would have used randomised levels and X-Com-like gameplay.

I love seeing this sort of material included in retro collections. It's easy to throw a few old games into an emulator and call it a day, but preserving gaming history takes more than making sure an old title still runs on a modern console.

Alien Breed was part of Team17's early identity, and this archive gives you a better idea of how the studio developed the series, what it was trying to achieve and how its ambitions changed as gaming moved from 2D to 3D.

The collection includes interviews with the original artists and developers, plus art, models, design docs, and even videos showing concept art progressing from sketch to final painting. Those cancelled games offer a wealth of content rarely seen in retro game collections, including level maps, concept art, and even gameplay demos.

The original games also get welcome additions that make them more accessible. Twin-stick controls are supported across the 2D and 3D titles; you can choose from display formats, CRT filters, and screen bezels, and save states mean you don't have to commit to a full session every time you sit down.

The collection also includes local co-op in supporting games, online Rush Mode and a new solo Horde Mode. These additions are useful, particularly if you want to play with someone else or fancy a more immediate arcade challenge.

I've spent time digging into the setup menus and fiddling around; for example, there's a choice of CRT scanlines, but also scanline transparency levels. There's no remake-versus-original graphics mode, because these aren't remakes but excellent emulations. I find the new DualSense control layout feels right; it's modern without ruining the series' distinct feel, and you still get that Alien Breed thing of hugging corridor walls.

There are some compromises, though. The original games have been preserved in their original formats, and while that's important, it also means some of their limitations come along for the ride. The 3D games in particular will test your patience if you're used to modern shooters because you need to play within the game's little 3D window (it's not as modernised as the Star Wars Dark Forces Remake, for example), and the collection could have done more to make those games 'modern'. But then that's the knife's edge a collection like this runs: we want the games we had 35 years ago, but we expect today's features; we can't have it both ways.

As a fan back in the day, I love having all these games together on a modern console, partly because they're still good, but also because I never got to play the 3D entries. Alien Breed is an important part of Team17's history, and the collection does a good job of showing how the series evolved across six releases.

But I don't think the games themselves have aged equally well. The top-down shooters still have something to offer if you enjoy old-school arcade games, with Alien Breed II being the one I've been returning to more than the others. The 3D games are more difficult to recommend as anything other than historical curiosities.

But it's the archive that makes this collection worthwhile. The artwork, interviews and unreleased projects give Alien Breed a context that simply playing the games can't provide. It's a chance to look at a British studio's creative development over an exciting period for gaming, a time when Team17 could have been swallowed but it thrived, and that's worth celebrating.

If, like me, you grew up with an Amiga, there's plenty here to enjoy. If you've never played Alien Breed before, however, I'd approach it as a piece of gaming history rather than a newly discovered classic because not every game in the collection is a banger.

#9038. Should I Exercise with a Phlegmy Cough? What You Need to Know

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

You’re feeling a bit under the weather, but you don’t want to lose the momentum of your fitness routine. So, should you push through and hit the gym, or is it better to rest and let your body heal? Let’s break it down!

Sleep is the best way to help your body recover quickly when you’re sick. But if you’re determined to rise and grind, you could use the “neck check” to decide whether to lace up those sneakers or stay in bed.

Many sports doctors use this theory to say that if your symptoms are above the neck — sniffles, sore throat, or a mild headache — you’re generally good to go for a light workout. But if you’re dealing with chest congestion, a hacking or juicy cough, diarrhea, a fever, or an upset stomach, it’s better to take some time to catch up on your Netflix watchlist.

Big disclaimer: there’s little scientific evidence behind the “neck check,” so use your best judgment.

If you’re going with the above-the-neck rule, exercising with the following symptoms is probably okay.

Going super hard if you have a mild cold is not a good idea. But a light workout, like a walk or a chill Peloton sesh, can be a great way to stay active without overdoing it. Stretching or light yoga might also do the trick.

Stick to light activities like walking for most earaches. Avoid intense workouts like weightlifting, yoga, or pilates, as they can throw off your balance and put pressure on your sinuses, exacerbating the pain.

Light and short workouts are likely fine if your sore throat is mild and lacks fever, cough, or swallowing issues. Remember to stay hydrated — it can ease your sore throat and is beneficial during exercise.

Light activities like brisk walks or gentle bike rides can help for allergy-related stuffy noses. If your nose is blocked, stick to very light activities, focusing on breathing. Skip workouts if you have a fever, chest congestion, or a productive cough with phlegm until you’re symptom-free.

If you’re experiencing the following symptoms, the workout can wait.

Working out with a fever increases dehydration risk and can worsen the fever. Plus, fever saps your muscle strength and coordination, making you more prone to injuries. So, do yourself a favor and skip the workout until you’re back to normal.

An occasional cough is your body’s way of clearing out irritants, but a frequent or phlegmy cough could signal a respiratory infection like a cold, flu, or even pneumonia or asthma. While a tickle-induced cough isn’t a gym deal-breaker, a persistent one is.

Diarrhea and vomiting can dehydrate you, and physical activity only makes that dehydration worse. Feeling weak? That’s a recipe for injury. Plus, stomach bugs are highly contagious. If you feel antsy, stick to light stretching or yoga at home.

The flu hits your respiratory system hard, with symptoms like fever, chills, sore throat, body aches, fatigue, headache, cough, and congestion. If you’ve got the flu, take it easy and give your body some well-earned R&R.

Once symptom-free, ease back into exercise gradually. Start with less intense workouts to avoid overdoing it. As your symptoms fade, you can gradually return to normal activity.

Regular exercise may shorten recovery time, particularly for acute respiratory infections. Listen to your body’s signals to gauge your strength. If you’re still contagious, opt for home or outdoor workouts, so you don’t spread those germs to fellow gym-goers.

P.S. Check in with a healthcare provider if you’re unsure when it’s safe to start exercising again.

Logging on to socials today, there's no escaping AI content, and audiences are getting increasingly skilled at sniffing it out. Maybe it's a rogue extra finger, or a reality-warping background that raises alarm bells. But for Crystal Palace fans, a blatant misspelling of their own mascot is what instantly had fans questioning whether there was slop afoot.

Sadly, it's pretty unsurprising, as even huge iconic brands like Coca-Cola have been caught up in AI controversy. With slim regulation and the tools only getting more advanced, it seems AI content isn't slowing down – but neither is the backlash.

We are pleased to confirm that Selhurst Park is a candidate host venue for the FIFA Women’s World Cup 2035 🦅 https://t.co/EUw5OI8hgGNovember 23, 2026

Announcing that its home stadium, Selhurst Park, is a candidate host for the FIFA Women’s World Cup 2035, Crystal Palace's seemingly innocent post was pretty unassuming at first. It's only when you take a closer look at the finer details that things get questionable. Excuse me... who are the 'Eacles'?

Fans quickly criticised the design, claiming there was no need for AI in such a simple post. "Do we not have a photo of the f**king stadium, our media team is in the gutter," one dissapointed fan wrote. "Imagine not having a photo of your own stadium and needing to slop one," another added, while one noted, "This is such a basic level of graphic design that would’ve taken seconds to make."

With AI tools readily available and often integrated into our everyday creative software, it's no surprise that it keeps infiltrating our feeds. With brands increasingly squeezed for resources and time, quick AI image generation feels like the obvious choice, but here it risks sacrificing the quality of your content. What should've been a celebratory post about the Women’s World Cup then becomes a source of derision and disappointment, proving that sloppy AI shortcuts aren't without consequence.

#9035. Does Creatine Increase DHT? What You Need to Know

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

Ah, creatine! It’s a popular supplement promising muscle gains and enhanced performance. But as you’re hitting the gym harder and seeing results, there are some potential side effects to be aware of. Here’s the lowdown.

Creatine monohydrate is a naturally occurring substance found in muscle cells. It helps to produce adenosine triphosphate (ATP) — your muscles’ go-to fuel when working hard.

Although you can find creatine in foods like red meat and seafood, many gym enthusiasts and athletes boost their stores with supplements. Why? Because more creatine equals more ATP, which means more energy for high-intensity activities. More fuel means more mileage!

Now, here’s where things get hairy. You might dial up your body’s DHT (dihydrotestosterone) production when you uplevel creatine. DHT is a derivative of testosterone and plays a big-league role in developing male characteristics. But here’s the catch: while DHT might beef up your alpha vibe, it’s also notorious for thinning out hairlines in peeps predisposed to male pattern baldness.

So, do creatine supplements cause baldness? Maybe! The buzz mainly stems from a small 2009 study where college-aged rugby players loaded up on creatine and saw their DHT levels increase significantly.

Because DHT can shrink hair follicles and shorten the hair growth cycle, it may seem logical to blame creatine for contributing to hair thinning. However, it’s important to remember that these findings are a one-hit wonder — they haven’t been seen again in other studies. Plus, let’s not forget that intense workouts alone can pump up these hormones, too.

As a result, the jury’s still out, making the creatine-and-baldness saga a hot topic for gym gossip and scientists alike.

The same 2009 study found that after a week of taking high-dose creatinine at 25 grams per day, DHT levels rose by 56%. When the researchers dropped the dose to 5g daily for two more weeks, levels remained 40% higher than baseline. These findings contrasted with the control group participants who took a placebo.

Does this mean creatine could spell disaster for your do? Well, creatine boosts DHT, the usual suspect in male pattern baldness, also called androgenic alopecia. However, your disposition to hair loss and the effects of DHT is genetic, meaning that it’s inherited.

Some folks are more prone to DHT’s hair-ruffling effects because of how their androgen receptor gene is wired. Hormones like testosterone and DHT bind to androgen receptors, typically triggering normal hair growth. However, variations in the AR gene make the androgens extra effective, making you more likely to experience hair loss.

So, while there isn’t much evidence to say that creatine supplements cause hair loss, the connection to increased DHT levels is worth considering if your family reunions look like a convention for bald eagles.

Beyond the potential for a breezy scalp, creatine is actually solid in the safety department, with long-term studies giving it a thumbs up. However, although creatinine doesn’t pose a risk to healthy individuals, it might not be your best move if you have kidney, high blood pressure, or liver disease.

Another thing to keep in mind is that creatinine loves to hang onto water, so expect some extra bloat and weigh-in surprises as your body adjusts.

Thinking of starting a creatine kick? Chatting with your doctor first is always wise, especially if you have other health conditions or take medications. They can advise you and rule out any potential interactions.

If you’re taking creatinine and notice changes to your hair, a check-up is a good idea. Shedding a few strands is normal, but it’s a red flag if you start losing clumps of hair. Rapid hair loss can indicate underlying health issues that go beyond your hairstyle.

Furthermore, consult a doctor if hair loss is weighing on your mind. They can offer solutions or treatments to manage your hair loss and stress.

Creatine is celebrated for its muscle-building prowess, but rumors of a link with hair loss exist. The good news is there’s little conclusive evidence directly connecting creatine supplementation to permanent hair loss.

However, creatine loading may boost DHT levels, a hormone linked to male pattern baldness, especially in people genetically predisposed to hair thinning.

So, if you’re concerned about hair loss, it might be wise to talk with a doctor before adding creatine supplements to your muscle-building routine.

#9034. Lisa Marei Schmidt appointed to lead Kunstmuseum Bern and Zentrum Paul Klee

Lisa Marei Schmidt has worked at other institutions including Kunstsammlung Nordrhein-Westfalen in Düsseldorf and Berlin's Hamburger Bahnhof

Photo David von Becker/Kunstmuseum Bern – Zentrum Paul Klee

Lisa Marei Schmidt has been appointed as the new director of two major museums in Bern: Kunstmuseum Bern and Zentrum Paul Klee. The board of trustees of the foundation that oversees both institutions selected Schmidt from 97 applicants following an international search, according to a release. She will lead on artistic direction and also chair the museums' management board.

Schmidt has directed the Brücke-Museum in Berlin, home to the world’s largest collection of works by artists from the German Expressionist group Die Brücke, since 2017. During that time she has co-curated exhibitions exploring complex and sometimes dark aspects of the history of German Expressionism, such as Escape into Art? The Brücke Painters in the Nazi Period (2019) and Whose Expression? The Brücke Artists and Colonialism (2021–22). Under her direction, the museum has also strengthened its work in provenance research, restoration, art education and digitisation. The German Association of Art Critics (AICA) named the Brücke-Museum as its museum of the year for 2023.

Born in 1978, Schmidt studied art history in Marburg, Amsterdam and Berlin, and curating contemporary art at the Royal College of Art in London. Before joining the Brücke-Museum, she worked as a research trainee at Kunstsammlung Nordrhein-Westfalen and served as a curator at Berlin's Hamburger Bahnhof from 2012 to 2017. In 2020, she curated Bonzo's Dream by Swiss artist Vivian Suter, which received AICA's Special Exhibition award.

“To me, museums are places where art and people meet,” Schmidt said in a statement. "They provide space for encounters, new perspectives and dialogue across society." She said she looked forward to getting to know the teams in Bern and building on the distinctive qualities of the two museums, which have shared strategic leadership under the umbrella foundation Kunstmuseum Bern – Zentrum Paul Klee since 2015.

Schmidt will also inherit a pressing challenge at Kunstmuseum Bern. In June, voters in the canton rejected a CHF15.7m (£14.4m) planning credit, or budget allocation, for a project to renovate the museum's historic building and replace its 1983 extension, with 51.8% voting against it. The museum says its ageing buildings still urgently need repairs.

Schmidt succeeds Nina Zimmer, who led the institutions for a decade and will become director-general of Vienna's Belvedere in January 2027. The foundation’s commercial director Thomas Soraperra will serve as interim director until Schmidt arrives.

#9033. Mondaine turns solar technology into design feature with Doppio Solar Skeleton timepiece

Swiss watchmaker Mondaine has expanded its Doppio collection with the Solar Skeleton, a timepiece that brings solar technology into the foreground of its design.

Rather than concealing the solar plates beneath the dial, the watch reveals them through a precisely cut circular opening, turning a functional component into a defining visual feature.

The design builds on the distinctive visual language of Mondaine‘s Doppio collection, which is characterised by double-line hands and indexes, a concave dial and a double-domed sapphire crystal.

Mondaine explained that these elements establish a sense of repetition, rhythm and structural clarity, while the exposed solar plates introduce an additional layer of depth and visual interest.

While solar technology is typically hidden from view, Mondaine has taken a different approach with the Doppio Solar Skeleton.

A carefully positioned circular opening around the centre of the dial offers a controlled view of the solar movement, while the outer section retains the indexes to ensure clear readability.

By making the technology visible, Mondaine aimed to bridge the watch’s technical function with its aesthetic identity, without compromising the “clarity and legibility” that define the collection.

Powered by a Swiss Ronda solar movement, the watch converts natural and artificial light into electrical energy, which is stored in a rechargeable battery.

According to Mondaine, a few minutes of sunlight can reactivate a fully discharged movement, while a full charge provides a power reserve of up to eight months in complete darkness.

The brand explained that this technology eliminates the need for regular battery replacements, offering a more resource-conscious approach to timekeeping.

The Doppio Solar Skeleton is available in two versions, each offering a different interpretation of its distinctive design.

The first combines a polished silver 316L stainless steel case with a vegan grape leather strap, bringing together traditional watchmaking materials and a contemporary material alternative.

The second features a polished black stainless steel case paired with a matching mesh bracelet, creating a more monochromatic appearance that emphasises the watch’s clean lines and geometric detailing.

Both versions feature a 41-millimetre case, a discreet date window and a precisely laser-etched Mondaine logo and solar markings.

A double-domed sapphire crystal and water resistance of up to 5 ATM complete the design, “combining refined aesthetics with everyday practicality”.

“With the Doppio Solar Skeleton, we wanted to make solar technology part of the design itself,” said Mondaine.

“By revealing the cells beneath the dial, we have created a watch where functionality becomes a defining aesthetic feature, while staying true to Mondaine’s principles of clarity, precision and Swiss design.”

The Doppio Solar Skeleton reflects Mondaine’s commitment to iconic Swiss minimalist design, where form and function work together.

By integrating visible solar technology into the collection’s established design language, the watch intends to demonstrate how a functional element can become an integral part of a timepiece’s aesthetic identity.

To find out more about Mondaine and the Doppio Solar Skeleton, visit the brand’s website.

For most beginners, an FDM (fused deposition modeling) 3D printer is the way to go. They're safer, cleaner, cheaper to run, and easier to post-process than resin printers. My exception to this recommendation would be if you specifically want to create detailed miniatures or character models, which require ultra-fine precision and a higher surface quality. For that, the best-value introduction is the Mars 5 Ultra.

#9031. 10 Signs You Might Not Really Be in Love: How to Tell the Difference

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

Love can feel like navigating a choose-your-own-adventure book with half the pages missing. Are you truly in love or just caught in a wave of infatuation? Sometimes, what seems like a heart-thumping romance may be a fleeting crush.

Wondering how to tell the difference? We’ve got you! Here’s a rundown of the 10 signs you’re not really in love.

Feeling a bit puzzled about your feelings for boo? That’s pretty normal. But before you start planning your future or picking out matching Halloween costumes, you may wanna make sure it’s real love and not a case of a serious crush.

Here are some signs that you may not really be in love:

Caught up in the romance novel vibe? If you’re all about the feelings of being in love rather than who’s sharing your popcorn, it might just be that you’re smitten with the idea of love itself.

Time to check if your relationship is more about the fairy tale than the real person.

Chatting with your partner shouldn’t feel as shallow as a kiddie pool. If deep talks are tougher than pulling teeth and rarer than a unicorn, it’s a red flag.

Sticking to small talk about the weather and dinner plans suggests the emotional depth for a lasting bond might be missing.

When discussions about future plans feel as far-fetched as sci-fi adventures, they may reveal underlying doubts about the relationship’s viability.

If imagining a future together feels unrealistic or undesirable, it’s time to ask yourself why. Real love plans a future; infatuation lives for the weekend.

Remember when their sock on the floor was cute? If little quirks now make you more cranky than charmed, it might mean the love goggles are off, your feelings have shifted from affection to annoyance, and the reality check has bounced.

Love is seeing imperfections and adoring them anyway.

Feeling more at ease or more ‘yourself’ when your partner isn’t around is a telling sign. If you’re secretly throwing mini-parties when they leave the room, you need to stop and think. Real-deal love means missing their chaos when they’re gone, not celebrating the silence.

Shared values are the anchor of deep, lasting relationships. If your core values clash more than a polka dot and stripes ensemble, you’re in for a rough ride, as finding common ground could be challenging!

Lasting love grows from shared beliefs and mutual respect, not from opposing battle lines.

No respect? No future. Respect is as critical to love as air is to breathing. Without mutual respect, you might just be coexisting rather than genuinely connecting.

If you no longer admire or respect each other’s opinions and choices, sustaining a healthy relationship will be difficult.

If they’re out of sight and totally out of mind, that’s not just independence — it might be indifference. When love is real, you should long for their laugh or lame jokes when they’re away. Could it be that your emotional attachment isn’t as strong as it should be for a lasting relationship?

If your best moments are consistently away from your partner, your heart might not be in it to win it. Perhaps your relationship isn’t providing enough support or happiness.

True love enriches your life and doesn’t play second fiddle to your social circle. It’s time to evaluate where your emotional energy is invested.

Still window shopping while you’re supposedly locked down? It’s a sign you might not be all in. A love that lasts doesn’t keep a backup catalog — it’s too busy loving what it already has.

Knowing why you’re still scanning for alternatives can help you address what might be missing or unfulfilled in your relationship.

Are you genuinely in love or just in love with being in love? If you’re secretly thrilled when they’re not around, stuck in surface-level chit-chat, or dreading deep-future talks, these are cosmic signs that it’s rethink o’clock.

Don’t ignore the signals — tuning in now can save you heartache later and lead you toward a love that genuinely fulfills you.

Last medically reviewed on June 26, 2024

We were genuinely impressed with some of the new AI features in Photoshop 2027, from Generative Restyle to Relight. But just a couple of weeks after its release, the latest version of the industry-standard image editing software is facing a reputational crisis.

The New York Times has banned freelance photographers from using the app because of a difficulty in knowing when it uses generative AI. That's just one publication, but the news has made a big impact, and the significance is clear: users may not be 100% sure when they are or aren't using generative AI to edit an image.

There's an easy solution, but will Adobe want to introduce it?

The New York Times wrote in an email to freelance photographers that the newest version of Photoshop “utilizes generative AI in ways that may not be apparent to users. Their use can result in metadata misidentifying photos as AI-generated.” As a result photographers have been told not to use the latest version of the software.

In photojournalism, it's an ethical issue. Images need to reflect reality, so editing is usually relatively limited. The inadvertent use of generative AI also brings with it the risk of an "AI content" tag on social media, which could lead people to question a report, and could severely damage to the reputation of both the photographer and any media outlet reporting news with an image flagged as AI.

The most obvious solution would be an AI-off switch. Digital artists, designers and those photographers who want to use generative AI tools in Photoshop could turn it on. Photojournalists, documentary photographers, and anyone who simply doesn't want to use generative AI or risk being shamed with an AI content tag, can turn it off.

Other software developers have done just that. Canva added an AI off Switch last week, and Maxon has included the ability to turn off its new generative AI features in Cinema 4D and ZBrush. It's a simple mechanism that can be flicked on or off at any time, and the gesture helps offer reassurance to those users who oppose AI.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

The question is whether Adobe will be willing to follow this lead, or if it will fear that a switch would call its direction into question or discourage people from using the AI tools it wants to promote.

Adobe didn't immediately respond to an invitation to comment.

#9029. Say What? 7 Tips to Unclog Your Blocked Ears

Earwax buildup, allergies, infections, or changes in air pressure might be behind your clogged ears. There are many easy ways to get relief at home.

Whether it’s from a cold, allergies, or changes in air pressure, blocked ears can disrupt your day-to-day activities and even cause discomfort. Thankfully, there are several effective methods to help unclog your ears and restore your hearing. Listen up!

Why are my ears clogged?

Clogging can happen either on the inside or the outside of your eardrum. Here are the most common ways your ears can get blocked:

  • Earwax in the outer ear helps prevent particles and excess water from entering the middle ear. However, if earwax builds up too much outside the eardrum, it can cause a blockage.
  • If you’ve been swimming recently, some water might be stuck in your ear canal, pushing against your eardrum. When that water hangs around too long, it can lead to a swimmer’s ear, an outer ear infection.
  • Sinus infections, ear infections, and Eustachian tube dysfunction can pressure your eardrum’s inner side.
  • Allergies can cause uncomfortable inflammation and congestion in your ears. Your sinuses, throat, and ears are connected, so when you feel stuffed up and sniffly, your inner ear feels the pain too.
  • Changes in air pressure, like when you fly, can cause uncomfortable ear pressure.

Best clogged ear remedies

1. Pop and unclog

The easiest way to unclog your ears is by “popping” them. Just pinch your nose shut, seal your lips, and gently blow. This simple technique, known as the Valsalva maneuver, won’t clear earwax or fluid but is a common trick people use on planes.

2. Swallow, yawn, or chew

The Eustachian tubes connect your middle ear to the back of your throat. They briefly open when you swallow, yawn, or chew. Altitude changes can cause these tubes to close, but chewing gum or yawning can help reopen them. Alternatively, you can try the Toynbee maneuver, where you hold your nose and swallow.

3. Ear drops

Over-the-counter (OTC) ear drops can soften and dissolve excess earwax. If you prefer a DIY approach, warm a small amount of mineral oil and use an eye dropper to apply a few drops into your ear for a few minutes.

Pro tip: Baby oil or olive oil can also be used, but make sure it’s not too hot. Additionally, diluted hydrogen peroxide drops can be helpful.

4. Warmth and gravity

To loosen up clogged earwax, use a warm, damp washcloth as a compress. Lie down with the clogged ear facing down against the heated washcloth. Gravity and heat will help the earwax move along more easily.

5. Hit the steam room

Steam can help drain sinuses and alleviate pressure in your inner ear. Close the bathroom door, let the hot shower run for a while, and then luxuriate with deep, cleansing breaths. 

6. Take allergy medication

Because your throat, sinuses, and ears are interconnected, any sickness affecting your sinuses or throat can also impact your ears.

Over-the-counter antihistamines, decongestants, or nasal sprays can relieve sniffles, coughs, and ear discomfort.

7. Rinse away the gunk

Rinsing your nasal passages with a medication-free saline solution can help reduce congestion and clear out mucus that might be causing ear blockage. You can also consider investing in a nasal irrigation system for more thorough mucus clearing.

When to see your doctor

Have you been unable to unclog your ears for a few days, or are you experiencing severe pain, fever, dizziness, hearing loss, fluid discharge, or unusual odor? If so, it’s crucial to contact your healthcare provider promptly. These symptoms may indicate an infection that needs medical attention.

What not to do when you have clogged ears

  • Cotton swabs: Q-tips and other cotton swabs to remove earwax can push it further into your ear canal, so don’t do it. 
  • Candling: Ear candles might seem like a fun party trick, but there’s no science to prove they work, and they’ve been shown to cause injuries.
  • Sprays: Decongestant nasal sprays can be helpful, but using them too long can lead to rebound congestion.
  • Drying solutions: A few drops of rubbing alcohol or a mixture of one part vinegar and one part alcohol can help dry out the ears when you have a swimmer’s ear. However, doing this regularly can lead to irritation.

Takeaway

Clogged ears are often caused by earwax buildup, allergies, infections, or changes in air pressure. You can use over-the-counter or DIY ear drops, irrigation kits, or warm compresses to unblock your ears. Antihistamines or nasal sprays can also help relieve clogs caused by allergies.

PSA: Consult a healthcare provider if your blocked ears are painful or at-home remedies don’t work.

Even if you haven't spent every waking hour of the past seven days immersed in the world of Leonida, you've sure seen a lot of the GTA logo lately. Along with the Vice City palette of pastel pinks, blues and sunset oranges, the logo has been everywhere, from developer Rockstar Games' billboards and murals to those GTA VI brand reactions.

For long-time fans of series, the GTA VI logo is a familiar design with the same core wordmark that's been in use since Grand Theft Auto III. But older readers who have never played GTA might also find it strangely familiar. That could be because it's based on a free typeface that was inspired by a very different kind of game.

The original Grand Theft Auto logo created by The Designers Republic for the first game's marketing featured cartoonish stars and flames for a '70s vibe. It was replaced by a simpler three-letter GTA logo for the second game, in the franchise. It was Grand Theft Auto III in 2001 that introduced the design we know today.

The logo is largely based on Pricedown, a free typeface developed by the Canadian designer Raymond Larabie and published by Typodermic. In his post about the history of the font on the foundry's website, Raymond says his intention was to closely reinterpret Pinto Flare, a display face made for Franklin Photolettering in the late 1960s and best known for its use in The Price Is Right logo.

"I kept the boxy structure and the odd unicase letterforms with swash descenders, but I drew my version harder and more angular compared to Pinto Flare’s softer feel," he writes.

Raymond says he released Pricedown on 30 November 1997. That was just two days after the first GTA came out for windows. And the coincidences don't end there. He says that when the font was later chosen by Rockstar's office in New York, he happened to be working as an art director at Rockstar Toronto. His colleagues weren't aware that someone working at the company had designed the font.

So the world's most expensive video game has a logo based on a free font? And it works: the chunky letterforms with their rounded corners work perfectly achieving easy readability while fitting into the rest of the game's branding.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

But it would be a simplification to say that Pricedown is all there is to the GTA logo. Ultimately, Rockstar modified the letterforms and arranged them to make them work as a logo design. The three words of the franchise's name are clustered tightly in an almost square block, the 'r' and 'h' conjoin, and a black stroke provides separation against coloured backgrounds.

Ink traps replaced overlapping curves, and the bowls seem to have been made more open to improve readability. This all helps the wordmark to function as a single cohesive unit.

An additional touch has been added for each game in the form of the numbering: a pink neon sign-like script for Vice City, tattoo-like blackletter type for San Andreas, the V that recalls US currency design for GTA V.

Considering Grand Theft Auto's satire of US culture and society, it seems fitting for it to have a logo inspired by the identity of one of the country's longest-running TV series (see our pick of the best GTA VI Easter eggs for examples of how the game references pop culture and its own legacy).

Looking for the font? The original Pricedown, now called Pricedown Black is available free for desktop use, and you can download it directly from Typodermic. Raymond later expanded the font into a complete typeface family with other weights. To use those, you'll need to buy a licence. You can find them at MyFonts.

For more on the game of the biggest video game in history, check out our interviews with Rockstar Games' art team on GTA VI's environmental storytelling and the building design in GTA VI.

#9027. Newly attributed Titian self-portrait, bought for almost $70,000 two years ago, on sale in London

The newly discovered Titian self-portrait

“Both Rubens and his erstwhile assistant Van Dyck venerated Titian as the very prince of painters.” So writes the Titian expert Peter Humfrey in the catalogue for Dickinson’s impressive new exhibition, Titian, Rubens, Van Dyck, which opened last night and runs until 18th December at 58 Jermyn Street, London.

Simon Dickinson and his son Milo have brought together two paintings by Titian, two by Rubens and nine by Van Dyck for the show, all from private collections and most for sale, priced between around £400,000 and over £3m. At the heart of the show is the relationship between the three painters, principally the influence of Titian on the two younger, Flemish painters.

The exhibition, one of the most ambitious staged by the gallery in its 33-year history, is accompanied by an extensive catalogue including essays from Humfrey alongside the Belgian art historians Koenraad Jonckheere, a professor in Northern Renaissance and Baroque art at Ghent University, and Katlijne Van der Stighelen, a Rubens expert.

While works by Titian, Rubens and Van Dyck are “very, very difficult to find”, Milo Dickinson says, there are still some at large thanks to all three being extremely prolific. “Titian was this great role model to Rubens and then Van Dyck, both as a man who was a successful artist throughout his life, courted by major patrons, but also as a painter: the colours he used, the compositions he devised,” Dickinson says. Rubens, for instance, “spent several months just copying paintings by Titian in Madrid, which had been bought by Phillip II of Spain.” As for Van Dyck, the sketchbook he took around Italy when he was a young man is full of annotated studies of Titians.

The exhibition includes several recent rediscoveries, most made after cleaning, with the catalogue outlining the arguments in favour of the attributions made by various experts.

Peter Paul Rubens, Study of the young Anthony van Dyck (around 1616-7)

Among them is what is thought to be a late self-portrait by Titian, variously dated by scholars to between 1546-47 to 1560. The attribution has been long debated by scholars, Milo Dickinson says. Everett Fahy, the American art historian and former director of the Frick who died in 2018, first proposed the attribution to Titian in 2009 when the painting emerged—filthy—from a French private collection. The oil on canvas, small at 44cm by 33cm, was sold for $69,850 at Sotheby's New York in 2024, catalogued as “attributed to Titian”. It has subsequently been cleaned, X-rayed and further studied. Now, Dickinson says, “various scholars—Peter Humfrey, Nicholas Penny and Ian Kennedy—have written on it and debated the dating of it because [if the attribution is correct] it would make it one of only three accepted self-portraits by Titian”, alongside those in the Gemäldegalerie in Berlin and that in the Prado, Madrid. The painting, which has been in a UK private collection since 2024, is now priced at £1.5m.

Another find is a Rubens head study which is now thought to depict a young Anthony van Dyck, based on dating, the sitter’s distinctive features and comparison with van Dyck’s self-portraits. The oil on panel, which measures 43cm by 35cm, was bought by the current owner at Sotheby’s Paris last November as part of the sale of the collection of the British property billionaire Manny Davidson. Catalogued as a Head Study of a Boy by Rubens, it sold for €744,000. With fitting circularity, Davidson had bought the painting as “attributed to Rubens” in 2007 from Simon Dickinson in 2007, who had spent several years trying to prove it was by Rubens.

The study had been thought to date to around 1614, when Van Dyck would have been only 14 or 15 years old, younger than the boy depicted here with his wispy stubble. But the Louvre, which holds the other half of this double head study, has recently argued that its sketch probably dates to 1616-17. “That got us thinking,” Dickinson says. “Once you've seen it cleaned, you realise the hair colour, the distinct shape of the face, the lips, the shape of the nose, they're totally concurrent with what Van Dyck looked like in his self-portraits.” He adds that Jonckheere and Van der Stighelen support the identity of the sitter as being van Dyck, alongside other scholars. The head study is for sale, price undisclosed.

Brunaille equestrian study by van Dyck (around 1629-32)

Yet another post-clean rediscovery is a study by van Dyck for the equestrian portrait of Albert de Ligne, Prince of Arenberg and Barbançon (around 1629-32) which hangs in Holkham Hall, Norfolk. It is one of several similar brunaille studies, one of which is the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York. Another of these sketches, presumed to be the original, had been in the De Craecker collection in the 19th century but had since gone missing. “Then this one appeared in an American private collection and it was pretty clear, upon seeing it cleaned, that this was the original and the other versions were copies done in Van Dyck's studio by assistants.” Dickinson says.

He adds that “the sheer quality, the way that he uses highlights, the abbreviated forms” in this version are superior when compared to the others. The pentimenti (revisions) in this, typical of Van Dyck, have also become clearly visible over time, Dickinson says, particularly the adjusted position of the horses head and front legs. The American collector, who bought it in 2014, is now selling the sketch through Dickinson, with an asking price in the region of £500,000.

At the top end of the price range is a friendship portrait by Titian, offered at £3m. Portrait of a young man with a gloved hand (around 1550) is thought to have been the portrait by Titian that is mentioned in van Dyck’s posthumous inventory. It was last publicly exhibited in 1939-40.

The exhibition will travel to New York for the Master Drawings New York art fair in (29 January–6 February 2027).

#9026. "Sacred" archaeological finds become raw materials for design in Ex Situ exhibition

New objects made from mammoth bone, leather from the middle ages and stumps from a road built under Roman Emperor Hadrian feature in the Ex Situ project, set to be exhibited soon in The Hague.

Initiated and curated by Dutch designer Marisa Klaster, working in concert with archaeologist René Isarin, the project makes use of materials that many in Isarin’s profession and the broader public might consider off-limits for new designs: the finds from archaeological digs.

However, while these finds, such as 40,000-year-old mammoth bone and 14th-century ship wood, sound like they belong in a museum, they are in fact deselected – not chosen for inclusion in any archives.

Deselected finds are duplicates, common in type, poorly preserved or otherwise judged to have limited future research value.

“The material that you see here is the lowest of the lowest quality,” said Isarin at a preview of Ex Situ at this year’s Dutch Design Week. “It’s not preserved. It doesn’t belong in a museum. It doesn’t belong in a depot.”

In fact, if it is not going to be used for educational purposes or reference collections, deselected archaeological finds are required by Dutch law to be carefully destroyed, as they are in many places around the world, said Isarin and Klaster.

Although the materials may be of low value to archaeology, the designers both found this something of a waste. With Ex Situ, they aim to explore a new category of use and preservation for these materials, believing artists and designers have the capacity to tell stories of heritage in a different way to museums.

With the permission of the province of South Holland, they gave deselected materials to nine Dutch practitioners with expertise in crafts such as ceramics, woodwork and glassmaking.

One of the most finished pieces, exhibited in a preview showcase at October’s Dutch Design Week in the Klokgebouw, was by footwear designer and materials researcher Judith Sanders.

She crafted the foundation posts from a section of the Roman Limes border road, dated to 125AD and built under the emperor Hadrian, into the heel of a pair of high-heeled shoes. Sanders was intrigued by the notion that they could perform structurally once again – this time bearing the load of just one person.

Bold numbers on the sides of the shoe denote where on the dig site the material came from, while a second pair of shoes works leather from the middle ages into a modern-day sneaker silhouette.

Another piece is by designer-maker Daan Simons, who worked with 14th-century wood fragments from a ship that was wrecked and then subsequently used in the construction of Rotterdam.

The texture and existing peg holes in the wood are preserved in his Remembrance Pots, which he imagines holding the ashes of a loved one or a keepsake of theirs, compounding the layers of memory in the vessel.

Klaster and Isarin started on the path to Ex Situ after meeting accidentally at their timber drying kiln, where she was having some wood dried for a furniture project, and he was having the deselected Roman posts dried in the hope they would find another life.

“Intrigued by their blackness”, Klaster asked Isarin if she could have them, and went on to make a series of tall vases. That was five years ago, and they have been discussing the potential intersection of archaeology and design ever since.

Klaster says that the Ex Situ designers were supported with information about heritage and the finds they were working with, but that the project naturally inspired some trepidation.

“In the work that they have made so far, you see that they have thought it through, and there is respect in what they made,” said Klaster. “But the first cut with a scissor or a bandsaw is, of course, a scary thing.”

“[One of the designers] was like, can I really saw that in two? And I said yes, you can. If you have a plan as a designer, yes, it’s yours.”

That worry will be echoed among some archaeologists, Isarin adds, and he and Klaster’s aim is for the exhibition to promote discussion among the profession.

“For archaeologists, this material is in a sense sacred,” said Isarin. “But it’s deselected, so nobody wants it.”

He said that while reactions have so far been positive, the issue becomes more thorny if the design were to take place in a commercial context – for instance, if Sanders’ shoes were sold by a fashion brand. In that sense, some archaeologists may see this project as opening a Pandora’s box.

“As soon as we enter the commercial world, then I think for many archaeologists it will be, even though it’s deselected material, an interesting debate ethically,” said Isarin.

“Suppose that all this matter, which has no value at all, that somebody gets rich out of it. That would be a disaster for many archaeologists.”

Nevertheless, Klaster and Isarin think it is a debate worth having.

Pieces in the exhibition come from practitioners ranging from glass artist Bernard Heesen, working with 17th- and 18th-century glass, to conceptual material designer Shahar Livne, working with mammoth bone, and ceramicist Lotte Douwes, working with Roman pottery.

“We have so much rich material beneath our feet, with amazing stories from 40,000 years up to today,” said Klaster.

The exhibition was previewed at Dutch Design Week, alongside the maximalist installation Everything Moist Seems Alive installation by Maison the Faux and Boris Acket and design collective Show Not Show’s Table of Power exhibition.

Ex Situ: Matter in Translation will be on at See Lab, The Hague, from 5 February to 7 March 2027, with discussion events as part of its programming. See Dezeen Events Guide for more architecture and design events around the world.

A will (technically a "last will and testament") is a legal document that specifies how your assets should be distributed after your death. It must go through probate — a court-supervised process that validates the will, pays debts and taxes, and distributes assets to beneficiaries. A living trust (specifically a revocable living trust) is a legal entity you create during your lifetime that holds your assets. When you die, the successor trustee distributes those assets according to the trust terms — without court involvement.

You need both: A trust does not name guardians for minor children (only a will can do that), and a trust only controls assets that have been formally transferred into it. A pour-over will acts as a safety net — it directs any assets not in the trust at your death to pour into the trust, where they are distributed according to the trust terms. The pour-over will still goes through probate, but it ensures nothing falls through the cracks.

The term "living trust" almost always refers to a revocable living trust — one you can change, amend, or dissolve at any time during your lifetime. You remain the trustee, manage the assets as you always have, and pay taxes on trust income using your personal Social Security number. For income tax purposes, a revocable trust is invisible — the IRS treats it as if it does not exist.

An irrevocable trust is fundamentally different. Once established, you cannot easily modify it, and the assets inside it are no longer legally yours. This permanence provides two powerful advantages:

The federal estate tax exemption is $13.61 million per person ($27.22 million for married couples) in 2026, but this historically high exemption is scheduled to sunset after 2025, potentially dropping to approximately $7 million per person. FIRE households who have built $3 million to $10 million in net worth through decades of saving and investment growth should monitor this sunset closely. If the exemption drops, irrevocable trusts become relevant at much lower wealth levels.

For most FIRE households with $1 million to $5 million in net worth, a revocable living trust provides the right balance of control, flexibility, and probate avoidance. Irrevocable structures become compelling only when estate tax exposure is real or asset protection needs are elevated.

Estate planning is governed primarily by state law, and the value of a living trust versus a will varies significantly depending on where you live.

Nine states are community property states: Arizona, California, Idaho, Louisiana, Nevada, New Mexico, Texas, Washington, and Wisconsin. In these states, most assets acquired during marriage are owned 50/50 by both spouses regardless of whose name is on the title. At death, only the deceased spouse's half passes through their estate plan.

The remaining 41 states follow common law (also called "equitable distribution"). Ownership depends on whose name is on the title. This distinction affects how assets pass at death and whether a trust or will provides better spousal protection.

Use this framework to determine whether you need a trust, a will, or both:

A revocable living trust is strongly recommended if:

Remember that a trust only controls assets titled in the trust's name. After creating a trust, you must fund it by re-titling your bank accounts, brokerage accounts, and real estate into the trust. Unfunded trusts — trusts that exist on paper but hold no assets — provide zero benefit. The pour-over will catches stragglers, but relying entirely on the pour-over defeats the purpose because those assets still go through probate.

The most common estate planning mistake with trusts is failing to fund them. Creating a trust document costs $1,500 to $5,000, but if you never transfer your bank accounts, brokerage accounts, and real estate into the trust, it provides zero probate avoidance. After signing your trust, immediately re-title assets into the trust name. Your attorney should provide a funding checklist. An unfunded trust sitting in a drawer is an expensive piece of paper — not an estate plan.

Yes. A pour-over will catches any assets not transferred into your trust during your lifetime and directs them into the trust at death. A will is also the only legal document that can name guardians for minor children. Every trust-based estate plan should include a pour-over will.

A revocable living trust prepared by an estate planning attorney typically costs $1,500 to $5,000, depending on complexity and your location. This usually includes the trust document, pour-over will, powers of attorney, healthcare directives, and initial funding guidance. Online trust services cost $200 to $500 but may not address state-specific issues or complex situations.

Yes, and you should be. With a revocable living trust, you serve as both the grantor (creator) and the trustee (manager). You maintain full control over all trust assets during your lifetime. You name a successor trustee who takes over only if you become incapacitated or die.

A revocable living trust does not reduce estate taxes — the IRS treats it as if it does not exist for income and estate tax purposes. However, a trust can be structured with provisions (such as an A/B trust or disclaimer trust) that maximize the use of both spouses' estate tax exemptions. For estate tax reduction, irrevocable trusts are the primary tool.

A revocable trust can be changed, amended, or dissolved at any time. You maintain full control. An irrevocable trust generally cannot be changed after creation, and the assets inside it are no longer legally yours. Revocable trusts provide probate avoidance and incapacity planning. Irrevocable trusts provide estate tax reduction and asset protection.

Without a trust, each state where you own real property requires a separate probate proceeding (called ancillary probate), multiplying costs and complexity. Transferring out-of-state property into a living trust eliminates ancillary probate entirely — the successor trustee can transfer or sell the property without court involvement in any state.

#9024. Are Tangerines Good for You? 5 Health Benefits You Might Love

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

Tangerines are not just tasty — they’re a powerhouse of nutrients. Packed with tangy flavor and vibrant orange color, these citrus delights offer a host of health benefits. From boosting your immune system to rejuvenating your skin, tangerines are nutrient-rich allies for your well-being. Let’s delve into their nutritional profile and discover why they’re a smart addition to your diet.

Tangerines are nutritional powerhouses. Here’s what each of these little champs pack under their orange belts:

Tangerines are teeny cousins of the orange but with a thinner, easier-to-peel skin. They boast a sweet and juicy flavor and pack a ton of vitamins, particularly vitamin C, as well as minerals like potassium, antioxidants, and dietary fiber.

These tiny bursts of sunshine have many benefits that can significantly enhance your health. Here’s why you might want to make tangerines a regular part of your diet:

Tangerines are loaded with vitamin C, turning them into tiny, tasty guardians for your health. This crucial vitamin supercharges your immune system by enhancing the function and effectiveness of white blood cells, which are essential for fighting off pathogens and infections. By improving the activity and response of these cells, vitamin C helps your body combat a wide range of infections more effectively.

Therefore, regular consumption of these mini-oranges satisfies your taste buds and boosts your body’s defense mechanisms — a win-win!

Want that glow? Tangerines have got you covered. They’re high in potassium, a real game-changer for regulating hydration and balancing fluid levels in your skin cells. This essential mineral keeps your skin cells plump and hydrated, warding off pesky, dry, dull patches.

Plus, potassium supports the removal of toxins and wastes, which means clearer, more radiant skin.

Tangerines are also a fantastic source of vitamin A, which strengthens the outer layer of your skin, smoothing out wrinkles and reducing fine lines. Along with vitamin C, it’s a potent antioxidant, protecting your skin from the damaging and aging effects of free radicals.

Are you having tummy troubles? Tangerines can help with a fiber boost that keeps things moving smoothly along your digestive tract.

These zesty little superheroes are your gut’s new best friends. They’re loaded with fiber that bulks up and softens things down there, making your bathroom visits smooth and speedy. This fruity fix helps manage everything from irregular pit stops to those bloated bleurgh days.

Fiber also balances your gut flora, promoting a healthy microbial environment in your intestines. This balance is crucial for optimal digestion, nutrient absorption, and immune function.

So, grab a tangerine to remedy your belly blues next time your gut feels out of whack.

Tangerines are a dynamo when it comes to battling serious health baddies like cancer and heart disease. These little orange wonders are loaded with flavonoids, natural compounds that help with heart health and cancer prevention.

Flavonoids help relax the blood vessels, lowering blood pressure levels and reducing the strain on your heart. This helps keep your ticker ticking smoothly and reduces the risk of cardiovascular diseases like heart attacks and strokes.

But wait, there’s more! When it comes to cancer, flavonoids mess with the bad guys — cancer cells — stopping them from multiplying and spreading their nonsense around your body.

Keep your peepers sharp with a dose of vitamin A from tangerines. This essential nutrient and compounds like beta-carotene shield your eyes from age-related issues and support healthy vision. It plays a key role in creating rhodopsin, a protein in your eyes that allows you to see in low-light conditions.

Munching on tangerines helps keep your night vision in superhero shape and supports overall eye function, keeping your peepers sharp and responsive.

Furthermore, tangerines contain other essential eye health nutrients, like lutein and zeaxanthin. These antioxidants are found in high concentrations in the retina, where they help filter blue light and prevent oxidative damage, further protecting the eyes from conditions like cataracts.

Sure, tangerines are delish and make your taste buds do a happy dance, but they’re also packed with nutrients that can seriously amp up your well-being.

From giving your immune system a high-five to keeping your heart beating like a healthy drum, tangerines are basically wellness wrapped in a bright orange peel. So, go grab one and make it your main squeeze!
