#9022. What's Love Got to Do With It? The Relationship Cycle Explained

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

Relationships aren’t just about candlelit dinners and cozy sofa nights — they’re complex AF, filled with ups, downs, twists, and turns. From the first flush of love to the settled comfort of commitment, relationships have stages that evolve with time.

Each relationship phase serves a unique purpose, helping you learn more about each other, yourself, and the kind of relationship you want to build. Understanding the dynamics of these stages is crucial for any couple (or throuple!) aiming to develop a lasting bond.

Whether you’re in the throes of a new romance or navigating the challenges of a long-term commitment, continue reading to learn how to rock each phase like a pro.

From those “can’t eat, can’t sleep” early days to the “let’s build an empire” moments, each relationship stage is like a season of your fave drama binge. But, like any good drama, the plot thickens as time passes and things change. Here’s what to expect, month by month:

Welcome to the love bubble, where everything about your significant other seems nothing short of magical. The positives overshadow any negatives, creating a blissfully skewed balance sheet of love. It lasts from about 6 months to 2 years for most peeps, but many folks say they are still madly in love even after 20 years together!

Research shows that during this stage, the prefrontal cortex, which is crucial for critically judging others, shows decreased activity. In other words, you’re less likely to focus on your partner’s faults and more likely to overlook their flaws.

Lurve also activates specific areas in the brain that are driven by goals and rewards. These areas are rich in dopamine and oxytocin receptors, chemicals that make you feel good and bonded to others. They encourage you to pursue and maintain a relationship because it feels rewarding and fulfilling.

If the euphoric stage is the wild, pulse-racing party of love, the early attachment stage is the cozy after-party where things get real comfortable. In the thrilling initial phase, your brain is doped up on dopamine, but as this initial buzz begins to mellow, a more sophisticated part of the brain starts to step up — the ventral pallidum.

Now, after the first year or so, deeper bonds are formed, helped along by attachment hormones like vasopressin and oxytocin, also fondly known as “the love hormone.” These hormones help transform the electric excitement of new love into a warm, enduring attachment.

Hold tight because the crisis stage hits around 5 to 7 years, and it’s a true test of your relationship’s resilience. This phase often feels like a rollercoaster, where life’s challenges can either pull you apart or push you closer together. Many couples experience a drift during this time, and how you handle it — either by addressing the issues head-on or continuing to drift — can define your future together.

Significant life events, like becoming parents, often occur during this stage and can intensify the pressure. These events can either strengthen your bond through shared responsibilities and mutual love or strain it to the breaking point. Successfully navigating this stage means moving beyond mere survival to fostering a deeper, more meaningful connection.

If you’ve made it this far, congrats, you’re in the deep attachment stage! Post-crisis, you’re looking at 7 years and beyond where you settle into that deep, comfy love. No more daily fireworks — now it’s about a slow-burning ember that warms the house.

You know each other inside and out, warts and all. It’s about unconditional support, knowing looks across crowded rooms, and being each other’s rock. Welcome to the good life!

Every relationship is a blend of sweet and sour and everything in between. Understanding the stages, from the initial euphoria to the deep attachment stage, helps you embrace the journey, keep your bond strong, and prepare your heart for whatever comes next. So buckle up and enjoy the ride — it’ll be worth it!

Senior Vice President Karen Robinson discusses Adobe’s Black Employee Network and the importance of representation.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

I recently had the privilege of attending this year's Adobe MAX, and amidst the flurry of excitement and innovations, what surprised me was the sense of community.

The phrase "finding your tribe" was thrown around profusely during the conference, and while I find the term mildly ickworthy, it bears truth. MAX is a space to connect, network, rant about the state of the creative industry, and, most importantly, a place to show up for your community.

It's no secret the creative industry was, and at times still is, a place of inequality. Be it race, gender, disability or age, while we have made strides to improve things, there are still gaps to be filled – something that Adobe is trying to address.

To learn more, I caught up with Karen Robinson, Vice President, Associate General Counsel, Litigation & Intellectual Property and leader of Adobe’s Black Employee Network, to discuss how Adobe is enacting change with purpose.

I've been at the company for about 14 years. BEN (Black Employee Network) started in the US, and I'm a founding member. Initially, it was an effort to build community, so we slowly started expanding. We had chapters in San Jose, San Francisco, Utah and Seattle, but then we started expanding internationally. Our largest community of Black Adobe employees is actually outside of the US, in the UK – BEN UK is a really strong presence.

I've been the executive sponsor for BEN for probably seven or eight years now, and it continues to be a focused effort that I'm really proud of. What's really interesting about BEN in particular is the allies. It's not just our Black employees – I love that there are so many people who get involved even when it's not necessarily part of their specific community.

It's about intersectionality. So, we have Access at Adobe, Asian/Pacific Islander at Adobe (APIA), Black Employee Network (BEN), Hispanic/Latinx at Adobe (HOLA), Indigenous/First Nations at Adobe (IFNA), Jewish Employee Network (JEN), Middle East/North Africa at Adobe (MENA), Pride at Adobe, Veterans Employee Network (VEN), and Women at Adobe. That's a really lovely thing about our Employee Networks in general, but I'm so proud of BEN. It's something that we put a lot of heart and effort into, and it sustains a lot of us.

We've always looked at inclusivity as something wildly important.

I'm responsible for some of our AI ethics and innovation, and as part of that, we made sure inclusivity is part of it. Looking at AI, how it can be used and what it's being trained on, if you're not focused on issues of inclusivity, you're missing out on large communities. That means the tools you're creating aren't serving those communities, so they're not the best tools you can create.

Our Employee Networks all developed out of a community's desire to be represented – to reflect their culture and the things they found to be important – and reflect them in the Adobe culture. The company really leans into it. It's not just ticking a box, or even just about minority groups getting together to have a sense of community. It's a way to make sure that we're offering the best products that reflect the communities we're serving. It's about empowering creativity for everyone. How do you do that if you're not including everyone?

Sure. You can look at the numbers. I'm not saying anything that's shocking or outrageous. There is still opportunity for more inclusivity within the broader sort of industry.

Something I didn't realise was how much representation mattered. It wasn't until I got to a point where I had people coming up to me and saying, "Hey, I, I didn't even realise that someone like you could exist at a tech company, it makes me think that there's room and opportunity and growth for me."

For a long time, minority communities were being told, "You need to be in science or technology." The reality is, you don't. There are entire swaths of the industry you can be involved in and not have a science or math background, but they needed to hear that and see that. I don't have a technical degree, and yet here I am – the first Black SVP at Adobe.

I look at the numbers, and we're growing. Success breeds success, and representation is a huge part of that.

#9020. Vibration Plate Benefits, According to a Weightlifting Coach

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

Vibration plates are like mini surfboards that give you a good shimmy while you’re exercising. Though you won’t find a mountain of extensive research behind them, you may be impressed by their possible benefits.

We asked a weightlifting coach to explain and show us how to add good vibrations to our workout routine.

These machines, which look like platforms or scales, are designed to activate something called whole-body vibration (WBV). WBV makes the body work harder by forcing it to contract muscles automatically.

Fans of WBV like to perform classic exercises on top of these machines, including:

Research points to WBV’s ability to boost blood flow.

Weightlifting coach Jarrod Nobbe explains that vibration plates help move blood by stimulating muscle contractions through rapid vibrations.

“The rhythmic contraction and relaxation of muscles help pump blood more efficiently throughout the body,” he says.

As Nobbe adds, movement generally increases blood flow and core temperature, preparing the body for activity. This means vibration plates may be an excellent warm-up activity.

A 2021 study showed that WBV can be an alternative exercise for older adults, boosting the effects of strengthening exercise.

Nobbe says this is because WBV engages muscles in a way that mimics resistance training.

“The vibrations activate and force muscles to contract and relax multiple times per second, which can lead to gains in muscle strength and endurance over time, especially when combined with specific exercises,” he says.

Nobbe points to some anecdotal evidence suggesting that regular use of vibration plates may help boost energy levels, possibly thanks to increased blood circulation and enhanced muscle activation.

“Ultimately, I stand by the idea that movement is medicine,” Nobbe says. “Tons of research already proves that regular physical activity boosts mood, mental health, and promotes energy levels.”

Nobbe says WBV may reduce muscle soreness, stiffness, and inflammation by encouraging blood flow to the muscles. This, he explains, aids in faster recovery post-exercise or injury.

WBV has been shown to improve bone mineral density, which Nobbe points out may positively affect those at risk of osteoporosis.

“The mechanical vibrations stimulate bone cells, potentially leading to increased bone density and strength, delivering the same positive bone health benefits of resistance training,” he says.

“Unfortunately, vibration plates aren’t a one-stop shop for weight loss,” Nobbe says.

He explains that vibration plates alone are unlikely to significantly reduce belly fat without dietary changes and additional exercise.

“While vibration plates can contribute to overall calorie expenditure and muscle activation, targeted fat loss requires a comprehensive approach including diet, cardio exercise, and resistance training,” he says.

These tips will help you stand on your vibration plate with a slight bend at your knee or perform exercises on top of it.

More research is needed around WBV — AKA what happens when you use a vibration plate — but existing smaller research is promising.

Use your machine carefully, and remember to maintain a healthy lifestyle and workout routine.

A nine-metre-tall replica of a town hall in Fayetteville, North Carolina, takes centre stage at American rapper J Cole’s world tour set, which has been created by production company Sturdy.

The set for The Fall Off Tour was designed by Los Angeles-based Sturdy to realise J Cole’s ambition to take his hometown, Fayetteville – or “the ville”– “to the world”.

To do this, the studio drew on the historic, two-storey Market House building, which has stood as a local landmark in the city since 1832. Sturdy created a weathered, ivy-covered replica of the structure, which is neoclassical with gothic revival details.

“The Market House was chosen because it’s an iconic piece of architecture historically as well in the town that J Cole’s from,” Martinez told Dezeen.

“I think a big part of the intention is that he takes home with him wherever he goes; conceptually, the idea was to take ‘the ville’ to the world,” he continued.

“And what better way to do that than something that lives basically at the centre point of the entire city?”

Other nods to the rapper’s life in Fayetteville include the presence of a Honda Civic car, which Martinez describes as a “supporting actor in the show”.

Positioned in front of the building at centre stage, the car is supported on ties that allow it to be suspended above the stage during specific moments of the performance.

“The car is like a supporting actor in the show that adds a little bit of an authentic take to the performance,” he said.

“His fans know the black Civic, and, at least from my perspective, with this being The Fall Off, the car needs to have a place in the story. It’s part of ‘the ville’,” Martinez added.

The set was designed by Sturdy to be easily dismantled, shipped and rebuilt between shows across the US, Europe, South Africa, Australia and New Zealand.

This determined the scale and design of the neoclassical Market House replica, which stretches just over 15 metres and is composed of easy-to-assemble wood and metal components.

The materiality of the structure also allows for J Cole’s performance to extend to the building’s first-floor terrace.

Alongside the structure is a 23-metre-long walkway lined with grass, rocks and a tree stump that doubles as a seat for the artist.

“Any show that we are doing, especially of this scale, has to be designed from a ‘rigging perspective’ to how this thing breaks down,” Martinez explained.

“That all has to be thoroughly thought out because we’ve got to be able to have the proper Legos. We can’t really just show up and hope that it’s going to piece together,” he added.

Also contributing to the set is a large LED screen, which, according to Martinez, is used “rather sparingly” throughout the performances to bring the stage design to the fore.

“I think for a long stretch of time shows were just about crazy visuals and putting stuff on screens and just letting people see stuff moving in the background,” he said.

“We never use the entirety of the screen for the whole show,” Martinez continued. “It’s to add a little bit of depth to what we have going on scenically on stage.”

J Cole’s The Fall-Off World Tour has been running since July, with recent shows at London’s O2 Arena. The tour will end in December in Johannesburg, South Africa.

Other set designs recently featured on Dezeen include Dave’s London show, which Stufish illuminated with a laser-shooting piano.

It's Thursday evening so Black Friday proper is upon us and the best Nintendo Switch Black Friday deals are already going fast in some cases. For us, anything below that counts as a proper saving. There are also plenty of strong game and bundle offers around for Black Friday. Below, you'll find links to all the best deals plus our rolling live updates as we continue to track the best Black Friday Switch deals through the evening.

Going by the last few years, bundles will probably rule Nintendo Switch Black Friday. When the consoles themselves barely drop in price, a bundle is where the real value is. Big console discounts rarely happen, even on renewed models, and sometimes not even then.

This bundle works out at just £10 more than the standard price of the console alone, and you get Switch Sports Resort, a game packed with sporting action for all the family, from tennis to archery and skateboarding.

This is currently the best deal for UK shoppers if all you want is the latest Switch 2 console. I'm not sure that we'll see much better than this, but we'll report here if we do.

So far, there have been some worthy savings this week – and actually some quite surprising ones. We didn't expect to see any discounts on the Switch 2 (we've spent long enough searching for paltry OLED discounts over the last seven years), but we have actually got some console deals.

In the UK? Find the Switch 2 for 9% less at Amazon – now £389.99.

If you're an early riser (wow, it's the middle of the night for you) in the US, you can also find a cheaper Switch 2 today, it's reduced from $499 to $469 at Woot (an Amazon subsidiary).

I don't think you'll find anything much cheaper over the weekend – though, of course, there's always hope. That's why we will still be here blogging.

If you've been tracking Switch 2 prices since it launched earlier this year, you'll have spotted that they haven't followed the usual slow downward drift. Instead, September brought a hefty price rise. So what happened?

The blame lies largely with power-hungry AI data centers. Throughout 2026, the big tech players hoovered up much of the world's memory chip supply, creating a RAM shortage that sent component costs soaring. Throw in a tangle of international hardware tariffs (and I wonder who we have to thank for those?!), and Nintendo's margins were suddenly stretched worryingly thin.

Rather than sell consoles at a loss, Nintendo raised prices across the entire Switch range. It wasn't alone either, as Sony and Apple have taken the same route.

The upshot? Expect some Switch deals this Black Friday, but bear in mind they'll probably be undercutting the September prices, not the original launch ones!

So, those are the console deals. But excellent offers on games and bundles are actually where it's at over these sales events. It's a fantastic time to stock up on games. Check out our Nintendo Switch game post to see a lot of those game discounts. And here are some UK game deals below:

Plenty of console bundles come with headline titles like Zelda and Mario, but the savings aren't always this generous. Take the Mario Party bundle at Very: it's priced at £451.99, which is only £24 below the RRP.

It's also a good time to upgrade your accessories, like cases, controllers and more. As a starter, there are some good deals on PowerA controllers at the moment. I love these controllers because they come in so many creative designs. There's something here for all types of fans.

For those awake in the US, there are bundle deals for you as well.

#9017. Hoor Al Qasimi to curate Venice Biennale in 2028

Hoor Al Qasimi, one of the preeminent figures of contemporary art in the Middle East, has been named curator of the Venice Biennale's next art exhibition, the Biennale has announced.

Following this year's edition, which was curated by the late Cameroon-born curator Koyo Kouoh, the appointment of Al Qasimi, from the United Arab Emirates (UAE), marks the second consecutive edition in which a woman from outside the Western art world has been chosen for the role.

Al Qasimi was born into the royal family of the port city of Sharjah and is the daughter of Sultan bin Muhammad Al Qasimi, the current leader of the emirate of Sharjah.

She has been involved in the Sharjah Biennial since 2003, when she curated the exhibition's sixth edition after completing her undergraduate studies at the Slade School of Fine Art in London. In 2009, she founded the Sharjah Art Foundation, a public art organisation that promotes and funds contemporary art collaborations in the emirate and internationally, including organising the Sharjah Biennial.

She holds board positions for numerous other arts organisations, including the International Biennial Association, Sharjah Museums Authority, Sharjah Architecture Triennial and University of the Arts Sharjah. She has also curated major exhibitions including the Lahore Biennale in 2020, the Aichi Triennale in Japan in 2025, and this year's edition of the Biennale of Sydney.

Pietrangelo Buttafuoco, president of the Venice Biennale, says in a statement that Al Qasimi's work gives “voice to stories and sensibilities shaped by research and the unexpected”.

He adds: “Her work brings together a profound attentiveness to deep-rooted memory and its legacies, an open perspective on the intricate complexities of the present, and a rare ability to listen to places and their people...These are qualities that we feel are particularly close to La Biennale’s vision”.

Buttafuoco, a right-leaning journalist and intellectual who was born and raised in Catania in Sicily, reportedly converted to Islam in 2015, adopting the name Giafar al-Siqilli (“Jafar the Sicilian”) in a reference to the Arab-Sicilian general associated with the Fatimid conquest of North Africa.

Since becoming president of the Biennale in 2024, he has sometimes championed art from the Middle East. In 2025, under his watch, Qatar announced it would launch a national pavilion at the Biennale. A temporary structure was used for the most recent architecture and art biennales; the completed pavilion building will be the first permanent addition to the Giardini, one of the Biennale’s two main venues, in 30 years.

In a statement, Al Qasimi says that the Biennale “continues to be a critical space to engage with the work of influential artists and curators”, adding that she was “honoured” to be appointed as curator.

Al Qasimi could not immediately be reached for comment.

Al Qasimi is the president and director of the Sharjah Art Foundation

From a Christie's exhibition to a posthumous display of Mel Ramos, this year numerous explicitly commercial shows signal a shift in attitude

Robert Storr speaks about his tenure in this exclusive extract from Massimiliano Gioni’s new book of interviews with biennale artistic directors

Collectors came out in force, but much of the art on show was not as exciting as that seen at Venice or offered by the auction houses

#9016. RIBA president rejoins ARB register to restore architect title

The president of the Royal Institute of British Architects, Chris Williamson, has decided to renew his membership with the Architects Registration Board, nearly a year after terminating it.

In a LinkedIn post, Williamson said he was rejoining the Architects Registration Board’s (ARB) register because he no longer wanted “to face the prospect of legal action”.

Specifically, he said he feared the potential “legal proceedings and financial penalties” from referring to himself as an architect, which ARB does not permit if a person is unregistered.

Williamson’s post comes nearly a year after he revealed he was not going to renew his membership to draw attention to what he called the “absurdity of the current regulatory framework”.

This ARB framework currently only regulates the protected title “architect” and the competence of those on its register, meaning it does not oversee the competence of unregistered providers of architectural services.

His withdrawal from ARB last year aligned with the launch of a campaign by the Royal Institute of British Architects (RIBA) calling for a new regulatory model for UK architects.

Though he has now rejoined the ARB register, Williamson said his position on the need to reform remains unchanged.

“Today, I have decided to rejoin the ARB register,” he posted on LinkedIn on Friday.

“Over the last year, I have sat in meetings and roundtables with Ministers, MPs and Peers, spoken at party conferences and COP31, and had the pleasure of awarding the Stirling Prize,” he continued. “Throughout, I have felt the fear of legal proceedings and financial penalties all for referring to myself, in these settings, as an architect – something that’s so fundamental to my identity.”

Williamson, the co-founder of Weston Williamson + Partners, began his two-year term as president on 1 September 2025.

In the LinkedIn post – a shortened version of an open letter shared with RIBA members – he said he will now continue to “push for a stronger system” for regulation.

The current RIBA campaign calls for three steps to reform architects’ regulation, including repealing the Architects Act – a UK law that sets the framework for the regulation of the title architect, under which ARB is the regulator.

It also proposes new legislation outlining reserved activities, such as submitting full planning applications, and who can execute them. The final step calls for the introduction of a Built Environment Council to oversee the competence of individuals and companies working in the construction industry.

“I know my decision to return may surprise or disappoint some of you, particularly those who followed my lead,” concluded Williamson.

“I want to stress this is not a step backwards and it does not reflect a change in my views. In fact, the year I’ve spent outside of the Register has only cemented my commitment to reform,” he continued.

“While my title may change, RIBA’s campaign for regulatory reform will not. I will use my experience on both sides to push for a stronger system that protects what we call ourselves – and what we do.”

Williamson was selected as RIBA president in 2024. Prior to this, he held several roles within the RIBA, including the vice president international from 2017 to 2019.

In 2014, ARB gave Dezeen 14 days to amend an article describing John Pawson as an architect, claiming it was “in the public interest” for Dezeen to use an alternative description, as Pawson is not registered with the board.

#9015. Toot Toot! 6 Tips to Prevent Protein Farts

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

Protein farts are a common, albeit smelly, side effect of high-protein diets. They happen because of how proteins are digested. But(t) don’t worry! We have some tips to help you say goodbye to those pungent protein toots without giving up your gains.

Protein farts are episodes of flatulence that don’t smell too pleasant! They’re generally due to upping your protein intake from supplements like protein shakes.

And while these butt whistles may be embarrassing, you’ll be glad to know they’re generally harmless.

Farts consist of different gases. The most stinky odors usually come from your gut bacteria, producing sulfur-containing compounds as they break down food. The main culprit is hydrogen sulfide, which gives off a characteristic rotten egg smell, yum!

But why do your protein choices lead to thunder from down under?

Well, there’s not much evidence that a high-protein diet causes protein farts. However, there’s some anecdotal evidence that supplementary protein — like protein bars, protein shakes, and powder powders — increases flatulence, but it’s likely due to non-protein ingredients like lactose.

Supplements containing whey protein or casein are derived from milk and are high in lactose, which can increase flatulence. If your body can’t properly digest lactose, it ends up in your colon, where bacteria feast on it, producing — you guessed it — more gas and cheek flapping.

So, whey protein can throw a curveball for those who are lactose intolerant or sensitive. Surprisingly, it might also stir up digestive drama even for folks who typically handle dairy like champs, potentially due to additives like fart-inducing sweeteners or thickeners.

Some people may also have more significant issues digesting protein. Proteins are big, complex molecules — breaking them down is no small task for your gut. Plant-based protein supplements, like those based on soya beans, may also worsen flatulence.

FYI: Another reason why flatulence is common with protein powders and supplements is due to the addition of artificial sweeteners in the powders and bars, like sugar alcohols, sucralose, sorbitol, xylitol, and stevia.

If you’re looking to continue your protein regimen without becoming a walking, talking whoopee cushion, here are some strategic adjustments you can make:

Don’t just dive into the deep end with your protein intake — wade in slowly. Gradually increasing the amount of protein you consume allows your digestive system to adjust without getting overwhelmed. This step-by-step approach can help minimize the likelihood of excessive gas.

Keep the water flowing. Drinking plenty of water is crucial as it helps your digestive system handle higher protein levels more efficiently. Proper hydration aids in the breakdown and absorption of nutrients, which can help prevent gas buildup.

Sometimes, your body needs a little extra help. Enzyme supplements like Beano or Lactaid can be game-changers, especially if you consume proteins that your body struggles with. These supplements help break down proteins and lactose, making digestion smoother and less gassy.

Variety isn’t just the spice of life — it can also be the solution to your protein fart problems. If whey protein tends to upset your stomach, explore other options like plant-based or animal-based proteins that might be easier to digest. Diversifying your protein sources can also ensure you get a broad range of nutrients.

What you blend your protein powder with can make a big difference. If you’re whipping up a protein shake, be mindful of adding high-fiber fruits and vegetables, as these can also increase gas production. Try to find a balance that allows you to enjoy the benefits of protein and fiber without the extra flatulence.

Introducing probiotics into your diet can improve your gut health, which can help manage and reduce gas production. Whether through supplements or probiotic-rich foods like yogurt, kefir, or sauerkraut, boosting your gut flora can aid in better overall digestion and less discomfort from gas.

Protein farts are a rather windy side effect of a high-protein diet, but they don’t have to knock you off course. Try easing into your protein consumption, staying hydrated, diversifying your protein sources, and integrating enzyme supplements or probiotics to max those gains, minus the stink bombs!

Abide's creative director, Jack King-Spooner, reveals the abject and uncanny side of stop-motion animation.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Stop-motion animation has been a popular aesthetic in indie games, giving creations a more tactile, handcrafted, and personal touch. But while many developers simply emulate this style digitally, two-person indie studio Talha and Jack Co prides itself on making real physical models. For co-founder Jack King-Spooner, creative director of the upcoming game Abide, it's always been what matters most.

"From studying art, I had just so much more affinity for tangible things and seeing what the materials give me as I'm making things," he tells me. "From my first game 15 years ago, I've always been invested in tangible assets. I couldn't really be bothered drawing pixel art when I could just make a little model and then photograph it from different angles, move it a little bit. It was just so much quicker for me."

While Talha & Jack Co's previous two games, the Scottish pagan action-adventure Judero and the chill post-apocalyptic robot-mining adventure Mashina, were sprite-based, Abide is more ambitious: a first-person 3D game, so they're scanning the epoxy clay models with photogrammetry, though cutscenes are still being created as stop-motion animation.

"The models are much, much bigger; they've got so much more detail," King-Spooner says, while bringing up a model in his hand as close up to the camera during our video call so that I can see the latex allowing for very realistic textures of skin pores and lips. "I'm always pushing myself with techniques, and finding new ways to do things. A lot of artists become frozen and immobilised with their craft because they think that there's a right way of doing things, whereas I just like doing things however I can."

Some of that detail nonetheless does have to be reduced, as a larger, more detailed model could be the equivalent of a super high-res model with 500,000 polygons. "We cut down to like 6,000 polygons so that we can hit good frame rates. They're a bit chunky, but for me they only needed to be recognisable as the same character as in the stop-motion cutscenes. I know lots of people love really tight graphics, but I'd rather spend the time on engaging story and engaging gameplay."

There are also additional parts that are made for the stop-motion cutscenes. For example, in a scene that requires a close-up of a character washing their hands, they use a larger hand for that shot instead of zooming in on the model's hands, then cut back to the normal model (something Thunderbirds' Jerry Anderson was famous for).

Even with games like Judero, the devs have noted that their stop-motion style has an inherent creepiness, so given that Abide is an "extreme stop motion horror" that includes prosthetic gore effects, King-Spooner is relishing that by doubling down on it. "There's something very abject and horrific about stop motion animation," he says, "It's got this nostalgia, but it's also got this kind of uncanny movement to it which you project life onto."

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

To an extent, it also feels like a deliberate response to counter the cosy perceptions people might have of this aesthetic. "A lot of handcrafted games are a bit kind of soft, aren't they? I think with Abide it's really nice that people will think, 'Oh god, a real person, this guy Jack is a real monstrous kind of person that he's made such perverted little dolls doing such horrible things!' I think it adds to the tangibility that it's very much a person's handiwork."

It nonetheless has an idyllic setting on the surface, set in the St Boniface retreat in the secluded countryside with a group of eight residents from different walks of life in some kind of need of them; at night it descends into full-on horror as you start sneaking around and explore parts of the house you probably shouldn't.

"One aspect which is very disturbing is they're all somehow reflections of myself," King-Spooner admits. "I think it's important for a creator to recognise that the work you output is somehow autobiographical of yourself. I'm just rather kind of transparent about it."

In many environments, King-Spooner has also opted to build physical sets or paint textures, such as splattering red paint to make wood textures look bloody or putting on muddy boots and trampling them on white paper to scan.

If there's a downside to creating physical models and objects, it's that there's often no room to keep them, so after production is over, everything is either chucked out or the clay is mushed up to be reused, although King-Spooner isn't especially precious about preservation. As he bluntly puts it, "We're all going to be dirt in the ground."

Abide is coming soon to PC, and you can wishlist it on Steam.

Alan Wen is a freelance journalist writing about video games in the form of features, interview, previews, reviews and op-eds. Work has appeared in print including Edge, Official Playstation Magazine, GamesMaster, Games TM, Wireframe, Stuff, and online including Kotaku UK, TechRadar, FANDOM, Rock Paper Shotgun, Digital Spy, The Guardian, and The Telegraph.

#9012. Undercuts for Women: Benefits, Styles, and Types

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

Is it time to give your hairstyle and scalp a breath of fresh air? Say hello to the undercut hairstyle, a fashion-forward solution that can elevate your look and promote skin health.

By significantly reducing hair volume, undercuts allow for improved air circulation around the scalp. The result? Less trapped heat and moisture — factors that can contribute to fungal infections, scalp acne, dandruff, and dermatitis.

Whether you’re battling irritation or want to give your “do” a new lease on life, continue reading to learn how undercut hairstyles can be your ally in style and scalp health.

An undercut involves shaving or cutting hair very short on the sides or back of the head while leaving the hair on top longer.

Originally popular in men’s hairstyling, the undercut has crossed gender boundaries and gained popularity among peeps seeking a hairstyle that stands out.

It’s a style that offers a stark contrast and is often used to add an edge to an otherwise conventional look. So whether it’s a side undercut, undercut pixie, mullet undercut, or nape undercut, these hairstyles for women, men, and folks of all genders enhance individuality while offering practical benefits like reduced drying time and less hair maintenance.

Choosing an undercut means embracing a hairstyle with a “heady” mix of aesthetic and practical benefits. Here’s why an undercut might be the refreshing change you need.

Ready to turn heads? The standout feature of an undercut is undoubtedly its unique appearance. Hidden under the longer layers, it packs a punch of boldness you can flaunt or conceal — whatever fits your vibe. You can control the reveal, whether you’re showcasing that edgy undercut for a night out or keeping it classy for the office.

Got a mane that’s more lioness than laid-back? An undercut might be your new BFF. Strategically shaving or trimming the hair short on the sides or back dramatically dials down the volume. This means your thick, voluminous hair becomes way easier to manage and style, turning a heavy head of hair into something light and breezy.

And the best part? You get to keep all the styling potential without any of the hassle. It’s a practical solution that doesn’t sacrifice style for comfort.

Are you chasing the clock every morning? An undercut could slash your prep time. With less hair to fuss over, you can breeze through your washing, drying, and styling routine faster than you can say “snooze button.”

This trimmed-down approach is a time-saver and reduces the daily wear and tear from blow dryers and straighteners, keeping hair healthier in the long run.

Undercuts reduce your scalp’s weight and improve hair follicle airflow. This keeps the scalp cooler and reduces the buildup of sweat and oil that can lead to scalp irritation, dermatitis, and dandruff. As a result, undercuts could lead to more robust, healthier hair growth.

Ready to shake up your style with a cool undercut? Here’s a rundown of some options to add a dash of daring to your daily look:

Are you looking for a dramatic change without total commitment? Try the side-swept undercut.

This style features a sleek shave on one side of the head, just above the ear, while keeping the hair on top and the other side longer.

It’s perfect for folks who love to play with contrast — sweep the top hair over to the shaved side for an instant bold statement.

If subtlety is more your speed, this undercut is a wicked choice. It’s a shaved area tucked away at the back of the head or underneath the top layer of hair so that it can play a fantastic game of hide-and-seek.

Wear your hair down for a business-as-usual look, or tie it up to reveal a sneaky, stylish surprise. It’s an excellent choice for peeps wanting a touch of edge.

Are you feeling bold and artistic? Design Undercuts take personal expression to the next level. These chic undercuts are masterpieces, boasting intricate geometric patterns, sweet floral motifs, or any design that speaks to you.

Do you prefer a more understated yet stylish look? The tapered undercut starts very short near the ear and gracefully lengthens as it ascends the head, blending with your other locks.

It’s a softer version of the undercut that pairs beautifully with bob or lob cuts and offers a gentle nod to the undercut trend without going full-throttle.

The undercut hair offers both style and substance. It reduces styling time and promotes scalp health. By alleviating the weight and allowing the scalp to breathe, undercuts can help minimize issues like overheating and irritation, especially during warmer months.

Whether you’re drawn to the edgy designs or the subtle tapered style, an undercut could be a clever hack to simplify your morning routine. More time for coffee, less time with the comb!

Last medically reviewed on June 30, 2024

#9011. IKEA's Color of the Year "unexpectedly fits in"

Photography courtesy of IKEA (unless stated otherwise)

Swedish retailer IKEA has unveiled its prediction for 2027’s Color of the Year – a dark, reddish-purple shade called Wild Fig.

Although revealed by IKEA US as part of its 2027 Style Guide, keen eyes would’ve already seen the shade pop up earlier this year in the sell-out floor lamp created by Dutch designer Lex Pott for IKEA’s PS Collection.

The company describes Wild Fig as “a deep, botanical shade with a rich purple tone”, although in certain lights, it looks closer to an earthy oxblood red.

“Full of character and the unexpected, it brings depth and a daring mindset to everyday spaces,” said Abbey Stark, home furnishing direction leader at IKEA US.

Used across furnishings and accessories, it can provide a subtle touch of colour without being overly aggressive, especially paired with warm woods and neutral shades, IKEA US suggests.

But the company equally pictures it being splashed across entire walls and argues it “unexpectedly fits in” with even brighter colours like baby pink and electric blue – IKEA US’s previous colours of the year.

The company’s Style Guide also pulled out a number of other interior design trends to look out for in 2027, including pattern clashing and Japandi minimalism.

Interior designers have already started making liberal use of Wild Fig, as seen in Note Design Studio’s scheme for the Lammhults showroom in Stockholm, where it blankets walls, floors and ceilings in the entrance, as well as an entire kitchen.

Other predictions for 2027’s colour of the year are set to start rolling in any minute, with Pantone’s set to be unveiled at the start of December.

Paint brand Dulux got ahead of the game when it named a muted green called Soulful Sage as its contender in September.

Some interiors industry insiders, including Dezeen columnist Michelle Ogundehin, have argued at least since the end of the pandemic that “it’s time to reconsider the whole colour of the year carnival”, which was originally invented as a marketing stunt for Pantone’s colour-matching system, much like the Michelin Guide was invented to sell more tyres.

#9009. Hickey Stages: Understanding and Managing Love Bites Effectively

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

Hickeys, or as scientists call them, subdermal hematomas, are love’s graffiti. If you’ve ever scrambled for scarves or turtlenecks, welcome to the kissing booth of knowledge! Join us as we navigate the lifecycle of hickeys, from their eye-catching start to their subtle fade, and learn how to speed up their departure.

A hickey, medically known as a subdermal contusion or hematoma, is simply a bruise that forms as a result of vigorous kissing or sucking on soft skin, typically around the neck. This intense suction causes the tiny blood vessels under the skin, a.k.a. capillaries, to burst and release blood into the surrounding tissues. The immediate result? An unmistakable red or purple mark that gradually shifts to a darker shade as it heals.

From a medical standpoint, hickeys are intriguing. They showcase the skin’s sensitivity and the body’s rapid response to minor vascular injury. Not so romantic when you think about it scientifically, right? But hey, it’s all part of the human experience of showing affection — or something like that.

When you get a hickey, your body starts a healing process that resembles how it deals with other bruises. Here’s a more detailed look at each stage of a hickey’s life cycle.

Immediately after the passionate moment, a hickey appears on the skin, screaming in shades of bright red or deep purple. This initial coloration is due to blood from the ruptured capillaries pooling beneath the skin’s surface in response to the suction. It’s your skin’s way of signaling that there’s been some minor internal damage in that area.

As the hickey begins to heal, it undergoes a whole wardrobe of color transformations, showcasing your body’s metabolic process at work.

Initially, the hickey darkens as the blood begins to oxidize. Then, after a few days, the body starts to break down and reabsorb the blood, so it turns lighter — going from blue to green to brown and, finally, mellow yellow. This rainbow journey reflects the breakdown of hemoglobin, the iron-containing substance in the blood, into biliverdin and bilirubin.

Finally, your hickey starts to ghost you. Over a week or two, depending on factors like your skin type, overall health, how severe the hickey was., and how your body rides the healing waves, the last traces of your hickey fade into nothing.

During this stage, the body’s immune system clears away the remaining by-products of the broken-down blood. White blood cells swoop in like a cleanup crew at a festival, gobbling up and digesting the debris in a process called phagocytosis, while increased blood flow to the area helps to flush out the remnants.

Need a hickey gone yesterday? Here’s how to help your hickey heal. Start with a cold pack — grab a spoon from the freezer or a chilled gel pack and gently press it against your hickey. This will help reduce any swelling and scatter the blood pooling under your skin, which can help minimize that bold bruise.

After using cold treatment for the first 48 hours, it’s time to turn up the heat. Switch to warm compresses to get the blood flowing smoothly again. A few minutes a few times a day invites more circulation to the hickey zone, helping you hustle through healing and clear out the blood remnants more swiftly.

You can also try a dab of comfrey ointment. Research shows it may reduce bruise size and coloration for some peeps.

Caught off guard? A little concealer or foundation over the hickey makes it less noticeable.

Not into makeup? Scarves and high-necked shirts are also great accessories for your camouflage arsenal.

Typically, a hickey will last anywhere from 5 days to 2 weeks, depending on its severity and your body’s healing capabilities.

Communication is key! Let your partner know your feelings about receiving a hickey — some might find it fun, while others may prefer to keep their necks clear.

While generally harmless, hickeys can sometimes lead to complications like skin infections or, very rarely, blood clots. It’s best to keep the affection gentle to avoid any issues.

Hickeys are nothing more than bruises in disguise. They start as bright red to purple love stamps and gradually fade over several days to a couple of weeks. Speed up the process with heat and cold packs or a splodge of comfrey cream.

Remember, the best approach to handling hickeys — like all aspects of relationships — is communication and care. So go forth, love responsibly, and keep a scarf handy, just in case!

#9008. Meet AMAA, Neri&Hu’s pick for the most influential architect of the next 20 years

Photography by Mikael Olsson unless stated

An innovative approach to the reuse of existing buildings defines the output of Italian architecture office AMAA, which Neri&Hu has selected as one of 20 names to watch in architecture and design as part of Dezeen’s 20×20 project, sponsored by Kohler.

Led by Marcello Galiotto and Alessandra Rampazzo, over the past 14 years AMAA has become known for its approach to the reuse of post-industrial structures in northern Italy, with the transformation of a former factory building into its own studio, a typical example of its approach.

According to Galiotto, these buildings are a taste of what the studio wants to achieve.

“What we have done in the past 10 years is really just a sketch of what we can do in the future,” he told Dezeen.

“Our research is still growing, and it can be applied to various programmes and contexts,” he continued, “but in 20 years we will both be 60 so we want the studio to be able to evolve and grow in new directions.”

The preservation and adaptation of existing buildings, which is central to AMAA’s practice, is a key reason why architects Lyndon Neri and Rossana Hu selected the studio for Dezeen’s 20×20 series.

“AMAA is significant for its fierce commitment to adaptive reuse,” said the duo, adding that the studio’s ability to repurpose historic structures “positions them as leaders in circular, life-cycle thinking in contemporary Italian architecture”.

AMAA is significant for its fierce commitment to adaptive reuse, [which] positions them as leaders in circular, life-cycle thinking in contemporary Italian architecture

Galiotto and Rampazzo met Neri and Hu when they participated in the 2023 Venice Biennale and have since been invited to host lectures at the University of Pennsylvania, where Hu is chair of the architecture department.

“We have a long relationship with Lyndon and Rossana who we consider to be both amazing people and great architects so it’s truly an honour to be selected by them,” said Galiotto.

Rampazzo added that she saw a clear overlap between Shanghai-based Neri&Hu’s work, which also has a focus on adaptive reuse approach, and their approach at AMAA.

“I’m a fan of their work and I see similarities in the way we do architecture and also the way we teach, despite our different cultural backgrounds,” she said. “I also love how they really support students and young architects by sharing their knowledge. We have a lot to learn from them but I hope we can have the same kind of legacy.”

Rampazzo and Galiotto have known each other for more than 20 years after meeting while studying architecture at the Iuav University of Venice.

The studio now has offices in Venice and in the industrial town of Arzignano, and has gradually become established among Italy’s most respected architecture firms thanks to projects such as their own office and a cafe housed within a 19th-century town hall.

We felt our education hadn’t provide us with knowledge of how to run a medium or large-scale practice, so my experience with Sou Fujimoto was about closing the gap between the present and future of our studio

The pair studied together at Iuav under the professorship of Massimo Carmassi, who they cite as an important influence on their approach to restoration and reuse.

After graduating in 2010, they assisted Carmassi and briefly set up a studio with friends to work on competitions. Then Galiotto went to Japan to work for Sou Fujimoto, while Rampazzo travelled to India for her PhD studies.

“We felt our education hadn’t provide us with knowledge of how to run a medium or large-scale practice,” said Galiotto, “so my experience with Sou Fujimoto was about closing the gap between the present and future of our studio.”

This global travel and work experience helped open their minds to alternative approaches and opportunities, as well as giving them the confidence to set up their own studio back in Venice.

“We’re still evolving, and evolving our identity,” said Galiotto. “But the important thing was to find ourselves. That’s why the path was complicated.

“Stay in Italy… going outside of Italy… travelling the world as much as we can to see things. That was the key, I think, to the position that we are covering right now in the panorama of architecture in Italy.”

In 2015, they opened a branch office in Galiotto’s hometown of Arzignano, which has been described as an “AMAA playground” due to the number of projects the practice has completed there.

Galiotto pointed out that their work in the town is part of an ongoing research into how architecture can blur the line between private and public spaces, with the Caffe Nazionale project providing a good example.

“Although the cafe is privately owned, it also forms the edge of a plaza so we wanted to give the space back to the people,” the architect explained, adding that the studio has coined the term “super public” to describe this aspect of their practice.

Alongside their work in Arzignano and Venice, AMAA now has commissions across Italy, including hospitality and residential projects, as well as schools and a theatre. Along with a focus on reuse, especially industrial buildings, Galiotto believes that the studio’s work is united by its considered eclecticism.

“We’re influenced by art, artists, travels and whatever we can be – by curiosity,” he said. “I would say it’s something that’s very important and it gives us this kind of eclecticism. Our architecture in this moment is very eclectic and at the same time has a strong direction.”

“It’s like a piano symphony, very complicated and very up and down, but at the same time very right like a poem, very well taught and very well executed, but very complicated in terms of ingredients.”

The studio’s expanding list of projects has caused it to swell in size to approximately 30 members of staff, which Galiotto suggested is necessary to facilitate their detailed, research-led approach.

We often collaborate closely with other architects, but we are also influenced by painting, sculpture and photography which enhances the eclecticism of our projects

Looking ahead, the architects said their main objective is to continue developing their team and consolidating their approach so that others can carry it on in the coming decades.

One concern they have is maintaining the same quality of output as demand for their services grows and they take on an increasing number of projects.

In just the past year they have completed 10 projects – as many as they delivered during the first decade of their practice – with public commissions now joining their work for private clients.

Despite the rapid growth, Galiotto and Rampazzo insisted their approach remains consistent whatever scale of project they are working on, whether it’s a chair, a public plaza or a museum, which they both agree would be a dream next project.

Asked for her view on the future of architecture over the coming decades, Rampazzo said there is a trend in Italy towards involving other creatives in the design process, which represents an alternative to the more autocratic approach of the past.

“Sharing ideas and opinions leads to more interesting outcomes,” she claimed. “We often collaborate closely with other architects, but we are also influenced by painting, sculpture and photography which enhances the eclecticism of our projects.”

In their teaching roles at institutions including Kent State University and Universidade do Minho in Portugal, Galiotto and Rampazzo are responsible for helping to shape the attitudes of the next generation of architects, who they recognise are entering the workplace in challenging times.

Galiotto said if there is one thing he tries to pass on to his students and the staff in his studio it is to “have passion and to keep pushing for what you believe in.”

“If you are humble, passionate and curious then you can find success,” he added. “Sometimes it can be tough, but when you love what you do you can live your life feeling like you never worked for a single day.”

To celebrate Dezeen’s 20th birthday, we asked 20 of the most influential architects and designers of the last 20 years to identify someone they think will have a major impact in the next 20 years. Over the next four weeks, we’ll reveal their picks in a series of profile interviews. The series is presented in partnership with Kohler.

#9007. The Critic as Artist (And Vice Versa): A Fireside Chat with Jerry Saltz

During Art Week NYC, a citywide festival organized by ARTnews, Artforum, and Art in America, I had the great pleasure of doing a fireside chat with New York magazine senior art critic Jerry Saltz.

Like many of us, Jerry has been skeptical of AI, so I started the conversation by reading him a description of his approach to criticism produced by an AI that was based on a talk he gave a couple years ago. After chewing on that for a few minutes, we went on to speak about how he became a critic, how he became famous on social media, what he thinks about art being produced today, his strong feelings about auctions (he despises them), and what advice he would give creative people.

We also touched on the recent documentary made about Jerry and his wife, the former New York Times chief art critic Roberta Smith. And of course, it wouldn’t be a conversation with Jerry without plenty of engagement with the audience.

Despite its myriad challenges, Jerry still believes in New York City as a center for artists, and as a place with a vital community. You can watch the full talk, which took place on Saturday, November 14 at the PMC Studio in Midtown Manhattan, via the video here.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In the world of movie posters, floating-head designs are among the most hated trends, and arguably no studio is more guilty of this creative sin than Marvel. Now, it seems it hasn't learned from its past, only doubling down on this disliked design with its new Doomsday poster.

Take a look at the best movie posters of all time, and you're unlikely to see a floating head. They're formulaic and overplayed, so it's no surprise that when Marvel dropped the Doomsday poster, fans understandably tore it to shreds.

Doomsday is already one of Marvel's most hyped releases since the End Game days, so you'd hope it'd bring a poster to match the energy. Instead, we've been blessed with a strange, overcrowded floating head design, muddied by an incessant shade of green.

"Bruh, this looks like the direct-to-video, bottom of the barrel s**t you saw at Walmart in 2004 and what you see on page 8 of your Prime Video search results," one scathing critic wrote. "Just ran my graphic design degree through the shredder cause nothing really matters anymore," a disgruntled designer wrote. "This is the worst poster I’ve ever seen, fan made ones are better than this trash," another added.

While it's disappointing that a huge studio like Marvel would resort to overplayed floating-head designs, previous variant designs and international posters have proved there's still creativity to be squeezed out of Marvel. (Hey, if we can't rely on the studios, there's an endless sea of fan-made poster designs that are far superior.)

#9005. Dead Man Is Accused of Stealing Art from Michigan Museums

The FBI is seeking a warrant to search electronic devices belonging to a Grand Rapids man accused of stealing art from two Michigan art museums. The news was reported by multiple outlets, including MLive.

According to a federal affidavit, Mikolai Augustine Stasiulewicz, 27, allegedly stole a color lithograph by artist Ellsworth Kelly, from Western Michigan University’s (WMU) Richmond Center for the Visual Arts on June 23. A worker notified WMU police that the work was missing, and Stasiulewicz, who was caught on surveillance video carrying the framed print, was identified through facial-recognition analysis by Michigan State Police. Related Articles 13th-Century Carving Stolen by Art Thief 'Eric the Belgian' Recovered in the UK Stolen Picasso Prints Found Under Pile of Clothes in French Riviera Apartment

Stasiulewicz is also alleged to have stolen a 16th-century Albrecht Dürer print from the Grand Rapids Art Museum (GRAM) on July 2. According to the FBI, he had been seen at the museum on June 17, “in what appeared to be a pre-theft surveillance visit.” Between the two thefts, he is accused of entering nonpublic areas at the Muskegon Museum of Art on June 25; however, Muskegon police said he didn’t take anything.

The FBI, which eventually took over the case, learned during its investigations that Stasiulewicz had met with a man on July 8 at the Gun Lake Casino Resort in Wayland, Michigan. Surveillance video shows him leaving with an unknown amount of cash.

Stasiulewicz was found dead in his home on July 30. According to the Kent County Medical Examiner’s Office, he died of a morphine overdose on July 26. Although the office’s autopsy report rules the death an accident, it also notes that “the decedent is currently under investigation by the FBI for involvement in an art gallery theft,” and that a brother had told police that may have played a part in his death.

Four artworks, including the Kelly, valued at $10,000 and the Dürer, valued at $10,000–$20,000, were found at the home the next day.

On Monday, November 23, the FBI sought a warrant to search Stasiulewicz’s cellphone and laptop computer to determine if any others were involved in the thefts. “In my training and experience, and that of the Art Crime Team, phones and computers like the devices will often be used to communicate with co-conspirators,” FBI Special Agent Evan Alkema wrote in the federal affidavit. “They may contain evidence of communications about what art pieces to steal, negotiations for sale prices, and arrangements to transfer and ‘fence’ the stolen works.”

Since its inception in 2004, the FBI’s Art Crime Team, which handles cases involving the theft, forgery, and trafficking of art and cultural artifacts, has recovered more than 20,000 objects valued at $1 billion.

Stasiulewicz was an amateur artist who studied at the Interlochen Center of the Arts, the FBI said.

#9004. HTA Design unveils "UK's largest council housing development"

A collection of brick-clad buildings containing over 450 homes forms Kidbrooke Park Road in London, which architecture studio HTA Design claims is the largest new-build council housing development in the UK.

Built on a formerly disused site in Greenwich, the development contains 452 homes, all of which are social housing.

Construction company Durkan delivered Kidbrooke Park Road for the Royal Borough of Greenwich as part of its council housing programme, Greenwich Builds.

HTA Design said the project “demonstrates what can be achieved when local authorities take an ambitious approach to housing delivery”.

“Our main goal was to demonstrate that council housing delivered at scale does not have to come at the expense of good design,” HTA Design managing partner Simon Bayliss told Dezeen.

“We wanted to create a neighbourhood where the homes are generous and adaptable, where landscape is integral rather than an afterthought, and where streets and public spaces feel active, welcoming and safe,” he continued.

“Together, the two phases have delivered the UK’s largest council housing development and one of the most significant social housing projects completed in recent years. We hope it serves as a benchmark for how future generations of affordable housing can be delivered across London and the UK.”

HTA Design recently completed the second phase of the scheme, which adds eight housing blocks with 330 homes to the three blocks completed in phase one.

Ranging from six to 15 storeys, the housing comprises one-, two-, and three-bedroom apartments and family maisonettes, most of which are dual-aspect.

The buildings at Kidbrooke Park Road have a reinforced concrete frame, clad in brick chosen to reference red-brick buildings in the local area.

Arched entrances, patterned brickwork and exposed concrete elements were designed to add visual interest among the development’s green spaces, which include tree-lined streets, community gardens, wildflower meadows, play areas and gardens designed for rainwater runoff.

“A key challenge was ensuring that two phases delivered separately would ultimately come together as one place,” said Bayliss.

“Through simple buildings and typologies with repetitive architectural components, combined with a landscape strategy that runs throughout the development, we set out to create a neighbourhood with a clear identity that worked within its context.”

Elsewhere in the development are a nursery, community facilities and green roofs. The housing is complete with air-source heat pumps, electric boilers and rooftop photovoltaics.

“We hope residents feel proud to live here,” Bayliss concluded.

“Beyond the homes themselves, the project has been designed to support everyday life, with play spaces, shared green areas, a nursery, community facilities and local amenities all contributing to a strong sense of community,” he said.

“Those are often the things that transform a housing development into a genuine neighbourhood.”

The deputy mayor of London for Housing and Residential Development Tom Copley said the project represents how London is “leading the way nationally on council home building”.

“The new development at Kidbrooke Park Road is the perfect example of what we’re achieving, with 452 council homes forming the largest single entirely new-build council housing development in the country,” he said.

“We recently announced that 60 per cent of the funding from the first round of the mayor’s new Social and Affordable Homes Programme will go to London boroughs, and we look forward to that decision delivering even more new council homes in future.”

Last month, the Royal Institute of British Architects (RIBA) announced the brick-clad Lion Green Road housing by Mary Duggan Architects with Ruff Architects, which contains a mix of private and socially rented homes, as the winner of this year’s Stirling Prize.

RIBA also awarded its Neave Brown Award for Housing to Rowan Court, a cluster of brick-clad social housing blocks in Seven Sisters designed by Satish Jassal Architects.

#9003. Bye-Bye Bites: 14 Ways to Get Rid of Mosquito Bites Overnight

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

Wondering how to get rid of mosquito bites overnight? Discover simple home remedies for quick relief. From crushed ice to aloe vera, explore easy solutions to soothe itching and inflammation for a peaceful night’s sleep.

If you’re caught without bug bite cream or ointment, don’t worry — plenty of simple home remedies can provide quick relief. From soothing aloe vera to the calming effects of oatmeal, discover easy solutions to alleviate itching and inflammation so you can sleep peacefully.

Just as you’d ice an injury, icing a bug bite can help decrease inflammation and temporarily numb the pain.

If icy cold treatments aren’t your vibe, you can apply heat instead to soothe your bump.

Aloe vera gel does more than soothe sunburns! It can also help ease bug bites and help them heal.

Baking soda can remove the itch. To make a paste, mix 1 tablespoon of it with a splash of water (not too much). Apply it to your bite as you would zit cream. Keep it on for 10 minutes before rinsing it off.

Did you know basil (yes, like the kind in your pasta) has a rich history as a skin infection remedy? It contains antioxidants that may bring down bug bite inflammation.

To whip up your own basil rub, boil a couple cups of water with 1/2 ounce of dried basil leaves. Cool the mixture before applying it to a washcloth and gently massaging it onto the bite for sweet relief.

You already know apple cider vinegar (fermented liquid from apples) is a huge player in the natural remedy world.

Some people use it to clean due to its antimicrobial effects, and others mix it into food or drinks for its possible health benefits (like helping with blood sugar issues).

Its beauty with bites is that it can help ease burning or stinging while disinfecting your scratchy little bump.

Onion juice (while not delicious) has antifungal and antibacterial properties, which could possibly help ward off infection. Plus, it could make your bite sting less. Just dab a bit of raw onion juice onto your bites. The downside? We’re not sure how well it works … and it’s kinda stinky.

Thyme has been used to help with skin concerns for a long time. You can use it to help decrease irritation by chopping it up and applying the teeny leaves directly to your bite for 10 minutes. You can also boil thyme, soak a cloth in the cooled liquid, and wrap it around your bite.

Peppermint oil may work as an anti-itch agent. Mix it with carrier oil (like olive oil) before applying it to your skin, though!

Another natural anti-itcher and astringent, lemon balm, may be helpful. You can either apply a lemon balm cream or chop up the leaves and apply them right to the bite.

Witch hazel is a natural wonder with many uses for skin concerns such as acne and psoriasis. It can tackle inflammation and burning while helping your bug bite heal.

This herb may work, but the science is a little dicey. On its own, arnica is toxic, so any over-the-counter products you find have been carefully diluted for your safety.

The yummy tea that calms and soothes at bedtime has many other uses, including potentially calming an irritated bug bite. Steep the tea bag for 20 minutes before squeezing it out and applying it to your bite once it’s cooled.

Blend minced garlic with petroleum jelly or fragrance-free lotion. Place the mixture on your bite for 10 minutes before removing it and applying a cool cloth.

Icing the bite for 10 minutes and then placing a mixture of baking soda and water on it for 10 minutes is a strong choice.

Though not tested for this purpose, some people turn to Vicks to soothe mosquito bites. It’s possible that its antibacterial and anti-inflammatory properties could help heal and soothe mosquito bites. But FYI, this product isn’t considered the best defense against mosquito bites.

Some toothpastes are cooling, so that sensation may offer temporary relief. Some people use toothpaste on insect bites since many toothpastes contain astringents, which can help shrink tissues.

Using repellent to prevent bug bites is a good idea. PSA: DEET and lemon eucalyptus oil are safe ways to repel insects.

Mosquitoes are low-key little monsters that cause the most insect bites worldwide. Most bites aren’t serious, but mosquitoes can potentially carry diseases.

Ointments, creams, or simple home remedies can help stop the pesky itch after bites. But remember that some natural substances can cause allergic reactions. That said, it’s always a good idea to do a patch test first.

#9002. Shahzia Sikander Sculpture in St. Louis Generates Protests and Counterprotests

Executive Editor, ARTnews & Art in America

Activists against women’s right to choose in relation to their reproductive rights protested a sculpture by Shahzia Sikander in St. Louis this week, calling for the removal of the 18-foot-tall work titled Witness (2023).

As reported by St. Louis’s First Alert 4, protesters associating the sculpture with pro-choice abortion rights gathered outside the home base of Rung for Women, a nonprofit devoted to women’s career development that hosts it. As the organization describes itself on its website, “Too many women are unfulfilled, unhappy, and underpaid in their jobs, but afraid to take the leap into the unknown. We designed a program to guide motivated women through a process to start working in exciting careers and get paid what they’re worth.” Related Articles Shahzia Sikander's Animated Film Selected for M+ Facade Commission in Hong Kong Shahzia Sikander Says She Won't Repair Beheaded Sculpture in Texas: 'A Testament to Hatred'

First Alert 4 quoted an activist with a group called Students for Life America associating Sikander’s sculpture with the overturning of Roe v. Wade in 2022. “Her skirt spells Hava, which is Eve, the first female rebel, to breathe life,” said Reagan Barklage, who related the work to the late US Supreme Court Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg. “It’s just, you do not need to kill your children in order to breathe life. That’s actually the exact opposite of what that means.”

She continued: “We’re alarmed that this is what they’re choosing to use to represent our city. We do not stand for these pro-abortion rights. And we’re trying to stand for women and true empowerment.”

A counterprotester thought otherwise. “We’re here because this organization that’s located on this block has every right to display whatever artwork they want on their own property,” said Leslie Zacks, who spoke of the protest in the context of a recently failed amendment that would have reinstated a near-total abortion ban. “The reality of the situation is that the people in Missouri have twice had the opportunity to voice their preferences with regards to the abortion issue and have made it very, very clear with increasing majority where their preferences are.”

Rung for Women issued a statement saying the organization “respects the right of individuals to express their views about art, including those that differ from our own. We recognize that Witness has prompted strong reactions and respect the sincerely held beliefs of those who have expressed concern. We remain proud to host this work by Shahzia Sikander at Rung for Women.”

The same sculpture by Sikander was the subject of heated protest in Texas in 2024, when it was decried by a group that called it “satanic” before it was to go on view at the University of Houston. After an opening and artist talk related to the work were subsequently canceled, Sikander said, “Art should be about discourse and not censorship. Shame on those that silence artists.”

An attempt by ARTnews to reach the artist was not immediately successful.

#9000. Tate Liverpool Plans Fall 2027 Reopening With Surrealism Survey

Tate Liverpool will reopen in fall 2027 after a £30 million transformation with the exhibition “Surrealism: Staging Dream Worlds,” a nod to the museum’s inaugural Surrealist show in 1988.

The surrealism exhibition will run from fall 2027 to spring 2028 and include works by Salvador Dalí, Eileen Agar and Man Ray. According to Tate Liverpool, the show will also explore the “important role of surrealism in the history of theater and dance” through the movement’s major commissions for stage sets and costumes. Also on view will be Dorothea Tanning’s costume designs for the ballet The Witch, photographs of Sheila Legge performing as the “Surrealist Phantom of Sex Appeal” at the opening of the 1936 International Surrealist Exhibition in London, and material from the archive of Ted Joans. Related Articles Meryl Streep Makes Big Donation to National Women's History Museum, Musée d'Orsay Receives Collection of Impressionist and Post-Impressionist Fan Paintings: Morning Links for March 19, 2026 Museum of Liverpool Evacuated by Phony Bomb Threat

“Surrealism invites us to see the world differently and what better way to reopen Tate Liverpool. This exhibition will spark imaginations, surprise visitors and reward curiosity, offering a fresh perspective on one of art’s most celebrated movements. It also brings a wonderful echo of the surrealist exhibition that opened our gallery in 1988, while taking visitors on an exciting new journey,” said Jemima Pyne, interim director of the Tate Liverpool, in a statement.

Tate Liverpool closed in October 2023 and was scheduled to reopen in 2025, but fundraising difficulties pushed the date back to 2027. The architecture firm 6a architects is redesigning the gallery’s home, an 1846 warehouse on the Royal Albert Dock, as part of a £35 million ($46.5 million) renovation.

#8999. L-Tyrosine Supplements: Benefits for Your Brain and Body

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

L-tyrosine is an amino acid (AKA protein building block) that supports your body, from your muscles to your noggin.

It’s a non-essential amino acid, which means your body can make it on its own, so you don’t have to get it from food

That being said, consuming foods high in L-tyrosine or taking supplements could have extra cognitive and physical benefits – here’s what to know.

L-tyrosine is an amino acid that the body produces naturally. Though your bod can prob create enough of the stuff on its own, some research suggests that supplementing with it can boost your mood and help regulate your stress response.

L-tyrosine helps make many vital chemical messengers, such as:

Supplementing with L-tyrosine is believed by some to boost levels of dopamine, adrenalin, and norepinephrine in particular.

Foods naturally high in tyrosine include:

L-tyrosine may improve your memory and mental alertness. Since L-tyrosine increases dopamine availability in your body, experts think it may boost your cognitive performance. In addition to reward centers, dopamine is linked to working memory processes and plays a key role in the brain’s aging process.

In a 2019 review of several studies, researchers found that a higher intake of L-tyrosine was linked to improved cognition. It also improved executive functions like brain flexibility, convergent thinking, and reasoning.

However, researchers noted that L-tyrosine is most effective when dopamine and norepinephrine levels are reduced (which basically means when you feel stressed AF).

Some L-tyrosine supplement companies claim that their products are both mood boosters and antidepressants, but the results are mixed.

L-tyrosine increases dopamine, the feel-good hormone that’s linked to reward processing and also addiction. In general, it’s been shown to be a vital regulator of mood, behavior, and brainpower – so it makes sense that getting enough of it could benefit your mood, too.

However, the research on supplementation of tyrosine for depression is super dated, so it’s challenging to draw any definitive conclusions RN. (Plus, depression is also a super complex condition that involves more than just dopamine depletion.)

And though there are some people dubbing L-tyrosine “natural Adderall” for its purported beneficial effect on ADHD, so far, there’s no research to support these claims yet, either. (Though it *is* true that there seems to be a link between ADHD and altered dopamine levels.)

Phenylketonuria is a rare genetic disorder in which the body can’t properly process another essential amino acid, phenylalanine.

Since those with the disorder may also be deficient in L-tyrosine, some experts think that supplementing with it could help relieve some symptoms like seizures or skin rashes.

However, according to a 2021 review of several studies, there is not enough evidence to say for sure.

The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) considers taking L-tyrosine supplements generally safe.

That being said, it’s not recommended to mix with the following medications:

It’s not advisable to take it if you’re pregnant or breastfeeding.

Research suggests that L-tyrosine supplementation likely benefits your brainpower under stress. It also may benefit conditions like depression, but more research is needed to know for sure.

Like any supplement, it is a good idea to contact your healthcare provider before adding it to your medicine cabinet, especially if you have preexisting health conditions or take medications.
